#1518. Manchester United: Ineos and Jim Ratcliffe are starting to annoy the Glazers

The start of the season is clearly not ideal for Manchester United. Only sixteenth in the Premier League with 7 points in 8 matches, the Red Devils are in a sporting crisis. A situation far from surprising, as the management of the English club is regularly criticized across the Channel. Owners of the club since 2005, the Glazers have not had very significant control over the evolution of the Mancunian club. If this was not seen directly when coach Sir Alex Ferguson was piling up victories in the Premier League, the situation deteriorated after his departure in 2013. Since then, chronic irregularity has affected the English team whose results and seasons bring hope before falling again after yet another disappointment. For 13 years, there has been a Europa League in 2017, two FA Cups in 2016 and 2014, two League Cups in 2017 and 2023 and the Community Shield in 2016. Which is light for an institution like Manchester United.

Glazer, Avram and Joel have long been targeted by supporters of the English club who demand to return to the top as quickly as possible. The club’s co-owners remain in the shadows, observing the evolution of their team from afar. It’s been since 2019 that Joel Glazer has not been to Old Trafford, it was during a match against FC Barcelona in the quarter-final of the Champions League. The latter was previously very involved and had a close relationship with Ed Woodward, the executive vice-president at the time. He had also pushed during the Covid-19 pandemic for all club employees to retain their entire salary. But since then they have withdrawn and this has intensified since February 2024.

A pivotal date for the management of the Mancunian club. Long looking for new shareholders, the Glazers allowed Jim Ratcliffe and his Ineos group to take 28% of Manchester United’s shares for 1.5 billion euros. A minority shareholding accompanied by control of the English team’s football operations. And this takes a negative turn when we see the current dynamic. “The fans were all singing about the Glazers, but I’m not sure they realize how bad Jim is. He couldn’t have orchestrated a worse situation. He was demoted in all departments. This is basically the opposite of what he announced as a strategy.» also confided a source from the English club to ESPN.

The American media is also wondering about the lack of reaction from the Glazers who remain the majority shareholders. Indeed, the value of the club is constantly falling. Almost three years ago, Jim Ratcliffe paid an amount of 33 dollars per share of the club. Friday on the New York Stock Exchange, Red Devils shares were trading at $20.61. A real snub, especially since Ineos’ choices are not paid for internally. Many recruitments for strategic positions were botched and 500 job cuts took place. Choices that did not please co-presidents Joel and Avram Glazer, whom they consider far from decency and their traditional values. Added to this is a drop in transfer and salary budgets. For the moment, the Glazers have not yet acted, but there is no doubt that Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos risk being held to account quickly if the situation gets a little worse.

#1515. Spalletti skips Fiorentina preview as Juventus seek a first win over Vanoli

Luciano Spalletti will not hold his eve-of-match press conference before Sunday's trip to Fiorentina. Juventus arrive on two straight wins, chasing fourth place, against a coach Spalletti has never beaten.

Juventus will travel to Florence without the usual preview from their coach. Sunday’s game at the Franchi kicks off at 20:45. The squad got back to Turin overnight from the Netherlands. The reason given is the club’s crowded run of fixtures, TuttoJuve reported. It is the last game before the international break.

The run began with a 2-0 win over Napoli at the Allianz Stadium on 1 November. Kerim Alajbegovic scored in the 70th minute. Aged 19 years and 41 days, no foreign player had ever found the net at a younger age in a Serie A game between Juventus and Napoli.

Four days later, Juventus won 2-1 away at AZ Alkmaar in the Europa League. Teun Koopmeiners and Randal Kolo Muani scored. The result takes them to 10 points from four games in the competition. After the match, Spalletti described himself as very pleased with a solid team display against strong opponents. He felt his side should have added a third goal.

The league position still needs work. The club’s stated aim this season is fourth place, and Como currently hold that spot. The defence gives some grounds for confidence. Going back to last March, no side can match the Bianconeri’s tally of 12 shutouts. Roma are next on 11.

Vanoli and Spalletti have faced each other only twice as coaches. Both meetings were Fiorentina-Juventus fixtures last season. Last November they drew 1-1 at the Franchi. Filip Kostic gave Juventus the lead before Rolando Mandragora equalised with a long-range shot.

The hosts’ struggles on their own pitch offer Juventus an opening against a side yet to find its footing at home.

The fixture carries plenty of history. Sunday’s game is the 175th Serie A meeting between the sides, according to the club’s statistical preview. Juventus have won 82, Fiorentina 37, and 55 have ended level. Juventus have scored 275 top-flight goals against Fiorentina. Two more would draw them level with Inter’s 277, the highest total by any side against the Viola.

Once the international break is over, Juventus’s next Serie A match is on 22 November.

#1513. Montpellier: the nugget Laciné Megnan-Pavé plays cash on the interest of PSG

This season, Montpellier is on track to aim for a return to the elite. With a 2nd place in Ligue 2 after 10 days, Zoumana Camara found the formula by surrounding himself with a few old hands to supervise an already successful and exciting youth. The economic context forced the club to turn to its training center and the lower divisions. This formula is working well for him at the moment. Better yet, this policy should last a little longer and perpetuate the MHSC, the management being in the process of locking out most of its young people, including the one who embodies this new wave: Laciné Megnan-Pavé.

At only 16 years old, and while he is discovering the high level this season, the striker has already scored three times in the league (plus 1 assist in 8 matches). While he had already signed his first professional contract last February, he signed an extension until 2029 last week. Montpellier is aware of having a real gem in its ranks. You have to know how to take care of it and protect it from the outside. La Paillade already experienced this this summer when PSG was ready to line up €15 million to attract him to their ranks. Laurent Nicollin had declined. “I do not set an amount because I am not a seller“.

“I didn’t get any more excited than thatreacts the player born in 2010, in an interview given to Midi-Free this Friday. I knew I was in Montpellier. I ignore all that. I was there to play and I continue with that in mind. I have a framework around me, my parents, the people around me, are there to manage this. They give me little feedback, but I’m not that concerned. What interests me is football, matches, training, my life in general.» Trained at the club and born in the capital of Hérault, it was not yet time for him to leave the cocoon.

“Montpellier has been my club since I was little. It’s rewarding to be able to play at La Mosson. The club’s interest in me is mutual. I love them as they love me. I didn’t want to skip any steps but play in my training club, get my own experience. We will see later what time decides», he continues, enjoying the discovery of the professional world. Elsewhere, he would not necessarily have had the same playing time, enough to convince him to extend. “I was asked if I wanted. Of course, I didn’t hesitate. I saw that I was starting to play, that there was confidence placed in me. It must be returned. It’s my training club, there was no need to procrastinate.“For a transfer, we’ll see later. His time will come soon enough.

#1512. Now will the FA put their money where their mouth is? England chiefs and UEFA must decide whether to back rival Japanese bid to FIFA president Gianni Infantino after slamming World Cup controversial sell-off plan

Published: 08:23 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 11:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

The FA and UEFA face a dilemma over whether to support a bid to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency after honorary Japanese FA president Kohzo Tashima announced his decision to stand.

Alongside the FA, UEFA have spearheaded opposition to Infantino following the collapse of his botched deal to sell stakes in the World Cup.

However, despite declaring Infantino 'has lost the confidence of UEFA' and threatening to boycott the World Cup, the European governing body have so far failed to come up with a candidate to challenge him at the March election in Rabat.

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin decided against a run for the FIFA presidency, opting instead to focus on securing another term at the top of European football.

At a meeting of the FA Council last month FA chair Debbie Hewitt demanded answers over the World Cup sell-off plan - and decision to suspend the ban of US striker Folarin Balogun after pressure from Donald Trump. She said: 'The man has to answer those questions, and if he doesn't answer those questions, no, he's not fit to be FIFA president, and that was what was shared in the meeting.'

But there is a growing feeling that a European candidate would struggle to secure sufficient support from the rest of the world, while Infantino believes he already has enough votes to secure re-election, making it difficult to find a credible challenger.

Japanese FA president Kohzo Tashima has announced a decision to stand for FIFA presidency

Tashima will run against the controversial current president Gianni Infantino (left)

That said, FIFA Council member and Japanese FA bigwig Tashima could split the Asian vote and is well respected in Europe.

With Tashima - the first candidate to secure the backing of a national association - declaring his intention to run, pressure is now mounting on the FA and UEFA to either support his bid or put forward a candidate of their own, having called for Infantino to step down.

It follows former Tottenham and Switzerland footballer Ramon Vega making a public leadership bid on Wednesday, though it is unclear whether he could obtain the backing of enough national associations.

Candidates require the support of five football associations to run for the presidency and must pass eligibility checks by November 18.

Tashima is the first candidate with a realistic chance to announce an intention to run before the November 18 deadline, where the support of five national associations is required.

Speaking to Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon, Tashima said: ‘I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association.

‘It’s not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world.’

#1511. Man Utd, the crazy week (which might not be enough)

We don’t know if this will be enough to save Michael Carrick’s place. But at least this Manchester United showed some heart in this crazy week. Winners of AS Roma in the Champions League (3-2) after being led 2-0, the Red Devils snatched a draw against Aston Villa (4-4), in a meeting where they were twice two goals behind.

It’s difficult to know whether to see the glass half full, or whether to remember the new defensive wanderings of the Mancunians, who made two disastrous starts during each period.

When he looked at his watch, Michael Carrick noticed that we had only been playing for four minutes, while his team had already conceded two goals: a strike from Alysson, who too easily deceived Senne Lammens (0-1, 1st), and a goal from Nicolas Jackson, the only one to feel the blow on a ball pushed back by the Belgian goalkeeper (0-2, 4th).

Man Utd therefore reacted for the first time, with a penalty converted by Bruno Fernandes, on a (rare) error from Boubacar Kamara (1-2, 16th), and a goal from Youri Tielemans (2-2, 44th). But the Red Devils shot themselves a second time in the foot, with a penalty stupidly conceded by Diogo Dalot, sanctioned by John McGinn (2-3, 48th), and a goal from Leon Goretzka, after a missed intervention by Leny Yoro (2-4, 53rd). This time it took less than eight minutes after returning from the locker room…

For what will perhaps be his last match, Michael Carrick managed to revive his team with his coaching, since it was two entrants who snatched the draw, Joshua Zirkzee (3-4, 90th+2) and Patrick Dorgu (4-4, 90th+6). So there is still a little life, but it remains a seventh match without a victory in the Premier League for Manchester United, well and truly relegated (18th) after this day.

#1509. Tragic Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel's family say they have an 'impossible void to fill' as his dad is comforted with devastated loved ones arriving at his funeral

Published: 07:14 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 11:29 EDT, 5 November 2026

Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel's family have said they have an 'impossible void to fill' as hundreds of people gathered to pay their respects after he was killed in a freak mid-match collision with a goalkeeper.

Mourners filled the streets of De Miguel’s hometown of Navahermosa in the foothills of Montes de Toledo, outside Toledo, where he was born and his family still live.

The 30-year-old Tenerife striker’s death after the on-pitch incident has stunned football-obsessed Spain and hundreds of members of the public turned out alongside his family and friends outside the parish church of San Miguel Arcángel.

The late striker’s body was delivered to the church in a black Mercedes with red and pink roses and flowers just before 2pm.

His devastated parents and sister walked directly behind, followed by his girlfriend.

Hundreds of mourners, including his team-mates, followed behind, filling the entire street with the procession.

The road became so packed that some were forced to spill onto a side road as grievers observed a few minutes of silence before the church bells rang.

Almost the entire village, some sporting UD Tenerife scarves, appeared to be in attendance and many wept as they walked into the church.

The church was so packed with mourners that at least 200 people had to listen to the service while stood outside.

One message written on a small banner tied around the flowers on the hearse said ‘our family won’t forget you’.

The rest of the town sat empty with shops and restaurants closed as the church service took place. His family began delivering speeches inside the church shortly before 4pm.

Their voices were heard breaking as they held back tears while they spoke. At the end of each one, mourners inside and outside the church erupted into applause.

After the 75 minute service his body was carried out of the church in a coffin by friends and family and delivered to Navahermosa Municipal Cemetery.

Devastated teammates embraced each other firmly as they left the church, with tears visible.

The rest of the town followed behind the hearse as the procession made its way through the back streets of the village.

Jesus de Miguel's family said the striker has left an 'impossible void to fill' as they attended his funeral

The father of tragic footballer Jesus de Miguel is consoled at the 30-year-old's funeral

The hearse of Jesus de Miguel arrives for the funeral in Tenerife

The family of Jesus de Miguel today released a statement about his death (Miguel is pictured with his sister, girlfriend, daughter and parents (Source: Instagram/martitamig)

Wreaths were laid outside the cemetery by representatives of most football clubs in Spain’s top divisions alongside a banner of him celebrating.

Hundreds of mourners entered the graveyard and dozens were in tears as they watched his body lowered into the ground.

The family released a statement this morning about their shock.

Seaking on their behalf, Manuel Hernandez said: ‘Jesus leaves a void that is impossible to fill, but also an immense memory in all of us who have been lucky enough to share our lives with him.

‘Thank you to everyone who has remembered him, to his team-mates, friends, fans and all the clubs who have wanted to convey their condolences and accompany us in this painful moment.

‘Feeling such love for Jesus and witnessing the impact he has had on so many people is something we will always carry with us.’

After this afternoon’s church service De Miguel’s coffin will be transferred to Navahermosa municipal cemetery, where he will be buried.

The funeral was taking place just two days after the 30-year-old tragically passed away following a collision with rival Andorra FC goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a Spanish second tier match.

The Tenerife striker was rushed to the Nuestra Señora de Candelaria University Hospital on Monday evening after receiving a flying knee to the chest from Owono, before succumbing to his injuries the following morning.

His girlfriend and daughter were watching from the stands as the episode unfolded, with paramedics attempting to revive him on the pitch as he went into cardiac arrest before being rushed to hospital.

His body was flown to the Spanish mainland from Tenerife last night.

De Miguel grew up in Madrid but kept close ties with Navahermosa, a town of just 3,500 people sitting 80 miles south west of the Spanish capital, where his parents are from and his grandparents still reside.

Fondly nicknamed Demi by locals, he maintained a tight knit group of friends in the village where he would spend summers as a child. More recently he would train on the municipal football pitch ahead of preseasons.

It was in the town that his father was watching the game at a bar and began crying after seeing the collision. He and his wife soon rushed to Tenerife after being told their son was in intensive care.

Real Madrid president Florentino Perez was in attendance and greeted mourners

Tenerife coach Alvaro Cervera arrives at the funeral in the striker's hometown of Navahermosa

De Miguel's Tenerife team-mates arrived at the funeral of the striker on Thursday

Spain's World Cup-winning manager Luis de la Fuente attended the funeral in Tenerife

De Miguel died on Tuesday morning after a horrifying clash in a Spanish second division match

Flowers and messages were left outside the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez Stadium in Tenerife

On Wednesday the town council declared three days of mourning, with flags flying at half mast at council buildings.

And fans will pay their respects on Saturday evening with a memorial service being held at the club’s Heliodoro Rodríguez López Stadium.

Tributes from across the footballing world have poured in since the tragedy.

His close friend Fernando Roman, who had been in contact with De Miguel's girlfriend, revealed she had been alone at the hospital before his parents arrived and has been hit 'very hard'.

Roman told Spanish broadcaster Vamos a Ver on Tuesday: 'Yesterday, my girlfriend and I were talking all afternoon and all night with María, his girlfriend, who was alone in the hospital.

'I've spoken with his girlfriend, and you can imagine how she is. Now we have to be with the family.

'We have to send our love to his family, to María, to his daughter Carla, who is a year and a few months old.

'It was unbelievable because we were talking about traveling to Disney with the girls, with my daughter too, and look what's happened.'

Roman also shared a letter on social media in tribute to De Miguel, reflecting on their friendship and stating he had 'brought happiness to everyone'.

'My friend... I can’t believe you’re gone... you have no idea how much I’m going to miss you. I didn’t just consider you a friend; I considered you a member of my own family,' Roman wrote.

'You were always there to help me when I was struggling—you were by my side during my worst moments.

'Many people didn’t truly know you, but having known you, I can say you were one of the best people I’ve ever had in my life: humble, hardworking, never one to look for trouble. You brought happiness to everyone around you, and above all, you were a truly good person.

'All the moments we shared keep coming to mind... that trip to Punta Cana with the four of us - a trip I will never forget... all the lunches and dinners we enjoyed together, the time we spent with our daughters, the escape rooms we both loved so much...

'In these difficult times for us, we want to sincerely thank everyone for the kind words and expressions of affection we are receiving.

'We don't have enough words to thank you for every message, every call, and every gesture of affection that we are receiving.

'Thank you to everyone who has remembered him, to his team-mates, friends, fans and all the clubs who have wanted to convey their condolences and accompany us in this painful moment.

'Feeling such love for Jesus and witnessing the impact he has had on so many people is something we will always carry with us.

'We understand the affection, concern, and support that her loss is generating, and we are deeply grateful. Jesus leaves a void impossible to fill, but also an immense memory in all of us who have been lucky enough to share our lives with him.

'Thank you for loving him, for remembering him, and for being with us. His family.'

'Tamara and I are absolutely devastated right now, but we know that from up above, you’ll still be with us—and, most importantly, with your daughter, with María, and with your entire family.

'My friend, I’m going to miss you so much... I love you dearly! REST IN PEACE!!'

Police investigating De Miguel's death are now probing the emergency medical response as well as the possibility rival goalkeeper Owono's horror tackle could be involuntary manslaughter.

It emerged on Tuesday that homicide squad officers based in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz had launched a probe as court officials explained any death 'not resulting from natural causes' automatically triggers a judicial investigation.

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono because the clash occurred during open play, although he is expected to be hit with a lengthy ban.

The goalkeeper shared a statement on Wednesday, revealing he is in 'enormous pain' over the death of De Miguel.

Owono said: 'These are being the most difficult days of my life. I am struggling to find the words and find it very difficult to assimilate anything that has happened.

'I feel an enormous pain for the loss of Jesús. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address; I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.

The striker was struck in the chest by Owono's flying knee as he attempted to clear the ball

De Miguel was rushed off the field on a stretcher following the collision with Owono

Close friend Fernando Roman (left) has revealed Jesus De Miguel's girlfriend Maria had been alone in hospital prior to de Miguel's death on Tuesday. Source: X/@ferroman9

'But right now, honestly, I cannot think of anything else except Jesús and the pain we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesús.'

Medical personnel involved in the footballer's care are expected to be questioned and detectives will sift through medical reports as part of the probe.

Equatorial Guinea international Owono, who has lived in Spain since he was eight, was red-carded for kneeing De Miguel in the chest near the halfway line late into stoppage time. The match was suspended when the two sides were drawing 2-2.

His club confirmed around had died at a hospital in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz on Tuesday morning, saying they were 'heartbroken' and had a 'lump in their throats'.

The club said: 'Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats, and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, which occurred this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8am.

'There are no words of comfort, there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow.

'We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire 'tinerfeñismo' community, who today mourn this cruel outcome.

#1508. Genoa 1-2 AC Milan: Five things we learned – battery life, the marksman and the core five

AC Milan managed to get the win that they needed going into the international break, but they certainly made hard work of it.

Things were going very well at the Stadio Luigi Ferraris against an in-form Genoa side, with Alphadjo Cisse and Christian Pulisic giving Milan a two-goal lead with less than 20 minutes on the clock. Both goals came from the high press, with Ruben Amorim’s side looking full of energy.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

However, as has been the theme this year, the Rossoneri were unable to turn it into a complete performance. The second-half drop-off saw Genoa build more and more pressure, with Ellertsson’s strike from range making it a nervy finish.

Milan held on to secure a win that gets them back into the top four for now, and the search for consistency can resume after the two-week break. Oli Fisher has five things were learned from the game at the Marassi.

We are running out of words to describe this debut season for Alphadjo Cisse. If it wasn’t certain from the sample size we had already, then the Bologna games and this one today were proof that he is a right-place, right-time player.

The young Italian was perfectly positioned for Rabiot’s pull-back in the opening exchanges, as he so often is. He ghosts into scoring areas and provides the killer touch, with the goal this afternoon being perhaps his most impressive so far: a first-time finish across his body right into the corner.

The cynical side of us wants to say that Goncalo Ramos could learn a thing or two about what spots to be in inside the box, though the defence of the Portuguese is that his movement often creates these pockets of space to attack.

Cisse is one of only three players born in 2006 or later to have scored 8+ goals across all competitions in Europe’s top five leagues. The others are Lamine Yamal (13) and Paris Brunner (8). He also matched Andriy Shevchenko’s eight goals in his first 13 games for the Diavolo.

Another remarkable stat is that the 20-year-old has scored his eight goals across all competitions from just 20 shots. Some might argue that kind of hit rate is unsustainable, but it shows no signs of stopping for now.

As mentioned in the introduction, the first-half performance from Amorim’s side was something that fans can really get behind. It was intense, aggressive and front-footed. The quality wasn’t always there to turn everything into danger, but the intent was there.

In fact, it was this tenacity that yielded the two goals. The first one came after Pulisic pressed and won back possession, allowing Rabiot to square for Cisse. Then, the press again forced an error from Genoa with Ostigard’s stray pass seized by Ramos, who squared for Pulisic to net.

It serves as categorical proof that something energy levels alone can be enough to get Milan into very good positions in games. Yet, we also saw the other side of things too: when the battery runs flat, the Rossoneri can lose control of games very quickly.

As a result of this, where more polished teams might see things out comfortably or even score more goals, Milan seem to sink into a hole of self-doubt, inviting pressure through a quite obvious inability to cycle the ball and keep opponents at bay.

Injuries are partly to blame for this, because not having versatile options like Fikayo Tomori, Samuel Chukwueze, Ruben Loftus-Cheek and Alexis Saelemaekers to bring on is hurting things. The bench on paper looked very weak, and those who did come in didn’t really help the chaos.

This is what Amorim refers to when he talks about the team not being ‘ready’. For various reasons – from the treatment room being full to the team not being fully cohesive – Milan’s level fluctuates wildly both within games and from match to match.

There was a report in La Gazzetta dello Sport this morning which highlighted a rather remarkable statistic. With Luka Modric, Mario Gila and Pulisic all not in the starting line-up, Milan are yet to pick up a single point.

This is arguably the crux of the rotation issue; the idea that managing the conditions of certain players is a necessity but upsetting the spine of the team is running a big risk. We’d like to add Rabiot and Diego Moreira into the mix too, as the five players Milan cannot do without.

The Spanish centre-back, the Croatian and French midfield duo, the Belgian wing-back and the American forward are simply too important. Their presence is vital not just because of their quality and propensity to provide decisive contributions, but because they are among the select group who can actually play Amorim’s way.

Each of them had a positive performance for various reasons. Gila’s fierce competitive nature facilitates the high line, Modric is the only one skilled in ball management, Rabiot is so wise when it comes to taking up the right positions, while Moreira and Pulisic are the technical sparks.

These are the players to build around from now until the end of season, while then waiting to see what the windows bring. When any combination of those five are playing, Milan’s limitations are often brutally exposed.

MilanNews described the performance from referee Davide Massa as a ‘disaster’, and we think that is being quite generous. The experienced official never once gave the impression of having control over a game where the pace and ferocity demanded it.

There is of course the one incident that everyone is talking about: the yellow card for Marcandalli after he brought Rabiot down. From our perspective, there are absolutely no doubts about it being a sending off.

The rules for DOGSO (Denial of a Goal Scoring Opportunity) take into account distance from goal, but the Frenchman and Cisse were about to have a two-on-zero attack with the entire half to run into. There is no way Ostigard was getting back to cover, and we question why VAR did not intervene.

To make matters worse, he then dished out a yellow card to Rabiot for rightfully protesting, and gave red cards to three of the Milan coaching staff too. In general Massa’s refereeing left a lot to be desired as there was no consistency in the fouls that he was whistling, and the five yellow cards the Rossoneri got felt disproportionate to Genoa’s two.

Thankfully the Diavolo were able to get over the line and bank the win, but if things had taken a more negative turn in the second half, we would be talking about that Marcandalli incident with a lot more venom.

Koni De Winter showed up in a big way against his old club, putting in another top performance in a week where he has been linked with a move to three big Premier League clubs.

Yet, we have to question the highs and lows. To best illustrate this, here are our ratings for the Belgian from each of the last four games.

vs. Bologna: Where to begin? I think he could have done better positioning-wise on Bologna’s first, with no one else to mark in the box, and then he completely gifted the free-kick that made it 2-1 for the guests. Some good moments too, but too many mistakes tonight. Maybe a 4.5?

vs. Inter (8): He absolutely won the battle against Thuram this game and it’s not like it was an easy one either. The two had several 50-50 duels and he always came out on top. Aside from his Thuram battle, he was very good overall and deserves a high rating here.

vs. Ferencvaros (5.5): That backpass for Torriani should never be played in that way, even if Maignan is between the sticks. He admittedly got a bit unlucky with his clearance in the second half, but even then perhaps he could have done better. Anyway, for me it’s the pass which brings his rating down.

vs. Genoa (7.5): The only poor moment came inside the first 60 seconds, when he was caught out a bit by a ball over the top, but he managed to track back and at least narrow the angle. After that, he was brilliant in his positioning, showing off with some great tackles and interceptions too. Really good.

Being the central centre-back is a position that carries a lot of weight and responsibility in Amorim’s system, and what is clear is that one game De Winter can look like the perfect man for the job, and in others he looks simply unplayable (and not in the good way).

One of the reasons for these wild fluctuations could also be because the former Juventus man simply hasn’t had a break. So, it is easy to see why the management are targeting a central defender ahead of January, someone who can give everyone a breather and help keep the levels high.

#1507. Spitting row mars feisty Millwall-West Ham clash

A spitting row marred the 100th Millwall-West Ham United derby and first for 14 years.

Taty Castellanos was facing trial by video after being accused of spitting on Filip Marschall during Saturday’s febrile 2-2 draw at the Den.

Millwall goalkeeper Marschall made the allegation to referee Paul Tierney, who was expected to include it in an official report that would then be assessed by the Football Association.

Spitting on an opponent is punishable with a six-match ban.

Telegraph Sport has been told West Ham striker Castellanos denies he spat on Marschall and believes he will be vindicated by video footage of the incident.

Lying little prick. Taty didn't spit ❌ pic.twitter.com/5vYxOtKqof

Millwall manager Alex Neil said after the game that fourth official Lewis Smith had confirmed a spitting accusation had been made.

Asked if he had spoken to Marschall about the claim, Neil replied: “I haven’t asked him about it. But it’s like anything else; I’m sure there’ll be footage of it, or not of it, if it didn’t happen.

“I’d be extremely surprised if Fil’s made an accusation and nothing’s happened. But that’s not really for me to deal with; I’m sure the authorities will deal with that.”

West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo said: “I’m aware of the allegation. I didn’t see the image; I didn’t speak with Taty. I cannot go much further on that.”

He added: “I’m going to try to look at the images.”

There were also ugly scenes at full time when players had to be separated at the end of a derby that had been at the centre of an unprecedented police operation.

There were six arrests as of 4pm on Saturday for offences including tailgating, assault on a police officer and entering or attempting to enter a stadium while intoxicated.

Eleven men were also arrested at around 7.15pm on Friday on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.

The group, believed to be Millwall fans, were detained in the vicinity of a known West Ham supporters’ pub in Stratford.

Saturday’s fixture was subject to a five-mile dispersal zone, the largest ever for a football match in London, with officers granted special powers to stop and search people and vehicles without reasonable suspicion and to remove anyone causing disorder.

Riot police were out in force outside the ground, with dog units and mounted officers among 400 personnel deployed – roughly quadruple the usual number for a game there.

Those and other measures – including the use of live facial recognition, a strict segregation policy and a 12.30pm kick-off to minimise supporters’ pre-match drinking time – prevented a repeat of the kind of violence which has marred this fixture down the years.

West Ham fans also received a police escort to a game that saw both sets of supporters hurl foul-mouthed insults at each other throughout.

Plans to keep rival spectators apart after the match were reportedly tested by scuffles that broke out as people left the ground.

If the police were ready for a fight before the game, West Ham’s players were not as Millwall tore into them from the first whistle and dominated a first half in which they scored twice through Caleb Taylor and Camiel Neghli and hit the crossbar through a stunning 35-yard strike by Mark Sykes.

MILLWALL STRIKE FIRST 🔥Caleb Taylor fires the Lions in front! pic.twitter.com/pPffYZD73D

However, the Championship leaders finally turned up in the second half and pulled a goal back through Mohamadou Kanté before Konstantinos Mavropanos equalised with just 10 minutes to go.

ALL SQUARE at the Den 🙌West Ham equalise in the 80th minute.Everything to play for with just 10 minutes remaining 👀 pic.twitter.com/qQmDlyuQmT

That was only after Marschall gestured that he had been spat at by Castellanos following a melee in the penalty area.

Tierney did, though, brandish a red card when Kanté pulled back Kyrell Lisbie as the substitute robbed him of the ball on the halfway line and ran clean through on goal.

The foul denied Lisbie the chance to hand Millwall their first win over their bitter rivals for 22 years, much to the frustration of fans who had roared them on from first whistle to last.

RED CARD 🟥West Ham are down to ten men, after Kante was sent off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity. pic.twitter.com/jRlVwLNiOs

Describing the atmosphere as “absolutely the best by far” since he joined the club almost two years ago, Neil said: “I told the players prior to the game that this game’s a real rarity and, as a player and as a manager, it’s a privilege to be part of it.”

Millwall: Marschall; Osei-Tutu, Taylor, Cooper, Sturge; Metcalfe (Servais 81), Mazou-Sacko (Cundle 90); Sykes (Baggott 70), Dykes, Neghli; Arconte (Lisbie 81).Booked: Lisbie 90+5.Goals: Taylor 16, Neghli 45+3.Subs not used: Batth, Crocombe, Doughty, Issoufou, Kelly.West Ham United: Hermansen; Walker-Peters (Kanté 46), Mavropanos, Kilman, Morato; Bowen, Engels, Mukasa (Austbo 68), Solomon; Piroe (Pablo 46), Castellanos (Orford 90).Booked: Morato 40, Pablo 83, Kilman 86, Mavropanos 90+5.Sent off: Kanté 89.Goals: Kanté 74, Mavropanos 80.Subs not used: Ajala, Austbo, Golambeckis, Herrick, Magassa, Scarles.Referee: Paul Tierney.

🗣️ 'We were able to bounce back, but we need to look at the things we have not done so well'Nuno Espirito Santo reflects on West Ham's performance after the Hammers fought back from 2-0 down to draw with Millwall. pic.twitter.com/NM1wQVcN0o

Asked by Sky Sports for his view on the “spitting” incident, Alex Neil said: “Fil [Marschall] was saying to the referee throughout the game when that happened at that point... Obviously I’m so far away it’s hard for me to see what happened, but I wouldn’t presume that Fil would say that without cause.

“I’m sure the referee and authorities who need to deal with it will look at it and, if it warrants it, it needs dealt with and then I’m sure they will.”

Lisbie darts to the by-line but his cutback does not make it through the thicket of limbs and West Ham clear their lines.

Millwall earn a free-kick to the left of the box as Mavropanos climbs all over Dykes. Servais picks out Baggott at the far post and his knock-down lands to Dykes who, will spinning, strikes the ball over the bar.

DYKES! 😱So close to a late winner for Millwall, but his shot flies over the bar. pic.twitter.com/fQFpQBdS7j

RED CARD 🟥West Ham are down to ten men, after Kante was sent off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity. pic.twitter.com/jRlVwLNiOs

Penalty shout! Metcalfe drives forward into the right of the box and Kante, who is hot pursuit, pushes the midfielder to the ground. Tierney immediately waves away the appeals and replays concur that the contact is probably not strong enough to warrant a penalty.

Bowen is presented with some grass to run into but his cross is well cleared. He gets another bite at the cherry, trying his luck from the edge of the box and Marschall just about gets to the rebound ahead of an onrushing Kante. A corner is awarded which the Millwall stopper flaps at but his team-mates are able to avert the danger.

West Ham earn a chance to deliver a corner from the near side but Engel’s inswinger finds Marschall’s gloves. Really poor.

Millwall continue leveraging Cooper and Taylor’s height in the box off set-pieces. Here, Metcalfe’s free-kick skims off the top of Cooper’s head but just misses the mark.

It looks like West Ham have gone to three at the back as Kante joins Mukasa and Engels in midfield. He’ll look to make late runs in behind.

Entering the West Ham box, he attempts to hold off Cooper but Osei-Tutu snaps in and earns a free-kick.

Two changes from Nuno, who takes off Piroe and Walker-Peters for Pablo and Kante.

Millwall have been good value for their lead, taking 16 shots and creating three big chances. West Ham, conversely have managed just one shot, off-target, despite controlling two-thirds of possession.

Arne Engel’s heatmap suggests he’s spent most of the match inside or just in advance of West Ham’s defensive third, which is not where Nuno will want either him or Divine Mukasa. The West Ham head coach could be tempted into changes at the break.

This is no more than Millwall – and West Ham – deserve. Sykes’s outrageous 35-yard strike deserved a goal and Neghli makes sure justice is served on the stroke of half-time. The roar that greets the players leaving the field is deafening.

The Den is in dreamland. Millwall take a two-goal advantage into the break and Neil celebrates with unbridled delight on the touchline. A caveat, though... Millwall did spurn a 2-0 lead in their most recent match away at Middlesbrough.

Millwall 2 West Ham 0 (Neghli) It’s come from yet another Dykes long throw, which West Ham have failed to clear. The ball falls to the feet of Neghli in the six-yard box and he spears the ball beyond Hermansen and Bowen on the line. And that’s the half.

"It's DREAMLAND at the Den!!"🫶🏼Millwall snatch a second goal before the break, as Neghli drills it home.An unbelievable half from the home side. pic.twitter.com/NIfSmwkHXh

Chance! Sykes from 30 yards strikes the ball cleanly and his ferocious effort beats Hermansen all ends up but ricochets off the woodwork and away to safety. Two minutes of time added on, by the way...

WHAT A HIT!! 💥Sykes' long-range effort RATTLES the crossbar. A potential contender for goal of the season, had that gone into the net... pic.twitter.com/ivBOslIZaO

Millwall, for the umpteenth time, find themselves in a two-vs-two situation on the beak, as Arconte tries to twist Kilman one way and then the other. He sets the ball to Metcalfe but the contact is not great and Hermansen gathers.

West Ham threaten Millwall’s lead momentarily as Mukasa breaks down their right, but Marschall does well to smother the ball and earns a free-kick on the process.

There’s a muted appeal for a penalty as Mavropanos nudges Cooper to the floor, but it’s a soft contact which takes place outside of the box anyhow.

Castellanos then attempts to burst down the right but Mazou-Sacko, who has been fantastic thus far, steams in and boots the ball out of play before geeing up the crowd.

Another foul... Osei-Tutu jumps into Morato but West Ham give the free-kick straight back to their opponents.

Morato leaves a leg in as Osei-Tutu attempts to break free, perhaps in retaliation to the earlier discretion, and he earns the first booking of the match.

It’s seven-seven in the fouls contest for those wondering, the latest being a mistimed challenge on Sykes by Castellanos near the right touchline. Millwall pump another ball into the box which is not up to much.

In an attempt to get his foot on the ball, Engels has often peeled out to the right-back position, but a wild, desperate cross-field ball that goes straight to Osei-Tutu sums up West Ham’s half aptly.

A wild challenge from Metcalfe on Cooper earns West Ham a free-kick and its then Sykes’ turn to land a late tackle, this time in the right channel. The subsequent delivery finds Castellanos but he cannot direct the ball goalwards.

West Ham’s strength comes from the fluidity of their front four, but Nuno’s creators have not been able to access them. So effective has Millwall’s back-line coverage been that West Ham have only managed low-quality final-third entries.

For the first time this half, Millwall begin to retreat deep into their own half, their lines of defence merging. And while West Ham tot up a fair number of passes on the edge of the box, they ultimately cede possession and Millwall spring a counter. Arconte appears to be through but Kilman does well to recover and Dykes’ subsequent shot is charged down.

West Ham are not learning their lessons and Sturge almost pulls off a similar pass in behind for Arconte, but the linesman raises his flag on this occasion. Replays show that it was really tight.

Millwall are going man-to-man as West Ham try to build and the visitors are struggling to get out. Sturge works infield from his starting perch on the left and almost threads a through-ball in behind for Arconte to gallop on to but Kilman does well to stick in a boot.

West Ham are desperately trying to calm this game down, but the Millwall fans are making that quite the challenge. The visitors string a series of passes together before Bowen strays offside.

Millwall then burst forward, Arconte this time popping up in a dangerous position on the right but Metcalfe fires over having picked off a loose Hammers pass out from the back.

Another Dykes throw-in sparks panic in West Ham’s box. Osei-Tutu’s back-post header appears to take a deflection off Walker-Peters, but the referee awards a goal-kick.

Millwall 1 West Ham 0 (Taylor) If at first you don’t succeed, try and try again... Dykes’ long throw from the right prompts chaos on the West Ham box and although Hermansen is able to keep out efforts from Sykes and Arconte, he can’t deny Taylor from close range. Cue bedlam in the stands. A massive, massive goal.

Or not… The Den erupts! That was appalling defending from a long throw and West Ham got exactly what they deserved, with Mads Hemansen’s brilliant save failing to spare them.

MILLWALL STRIKE FIRST 🔥Caleb Taylor fires the Lions in front! pic.twitter.com/pPffYZD73D

It is all Millwall so far. They have been first to pretty much every ball and are giving West Ham no time on it at all. Konstantinos Mavropanos has just bought the visitors a breather after going down injured.

Hermansen gets caught in no-man’s land as Millwall spin in another ball from deep. It falls to the feet of Dykes but his effort does not have the requisite power to beat Kilman on the line.

Mavropanos appears to have been taken out by his own goalkeeper in the commotion and receives some on-field medical treatment.

Neil will be happy with how his side have started this match. Their intensity off the ball has forced West Ham into errors and here Sturge picks Bowen’s pocket on the halfway line before picking out Arconte in the box. He tries to squeeze a shot through Mukasa but the young midfielder does well to clear his lines.

The resulting corner comes out to Mazou-Sacko on the edge of the box but his effort sails over the bar.

Dykes and Arconte are Millwall’s attacking threats and the former wins a free-kick in the left channel. The hosts load the box with their biggest aerial threats but Metcalfe’s teasing inswinger just evades everyone. Tierney blows up for a foul anyhow...

There’s a minor clash off the ball as Morato and Cooper exchange words. Paul Tierney speaks with both players before Dykes launches a long throw into the box which is cleared and Hermansen is wise to the subsequent cross off the second phase.

Arconte tiptoes into the West Ham box and picks out Sturge whose miscued shot finds Metcalfe on the edge of the box. His effort is straight at Hermansen who collects the ball calmly.

That Jenson Metcalfe tackle on West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen came after just 15 seconds. What Vinny Jones might call “a reducer”.

"That's the expectation, I would imagine" 😅The first free-kick is awarded just 12 seconds into Millwall's derby against West Ham.Watch it LIVE on ITV1 🎥 pic.twitter.com/qpxjQEKN6x

Millwall launch a free-kick from deep into the box after Castellanos gives away a needless foul and after some pinball Hermansen gathers.

It took just 13 seconds for us to get our first foul. Kudos to anyone who had that in their Dockers Derby sweepstake... A late lunge from Metcalfe on Bowen.

And the players emerge, Hey Jude now being played... Millwall are in their customary navy-blue home strip and white shorts. West Ham are giving their new white away kit a first outing.

There’s just about enough time for the two sides to meet for quick summits before Millwall get us under way!

The atmosphere is building nicely in the ground and the players are now lined up in the tunnel, Cooper and Bowen standing shoulder to shoulder.

Seats are filling up rapidly with barely 10 minutes before kick-off, with the away end a notable exception. The home fans are making their own presence felt as The Jam’s A Town Called Malice and The Clash’s London Calling blare out over the public-address system.

"The fans are up for it, the players are up for it" 💪🏼Lyndon Dykes looks ahead to today's match, and reflects on his strong start to life as a Millwall player.Watch it LIVE on ITV1 🎥 pic.twitter.com/V9nPzbh3Ob

Kevin Nolan, West Ham’s captain, was sent off early but his team-mates defied the odds to win 2-1 thanks to goals from Carlton Cole and Winston Reid either side of a stunning Liam Trotter strike.

In Millwall’s match-day squad that day were… Harry Kane and Ryan Mason.

The last time West Ham and Millwall met, Harry Kane was a Millwall player 😅This is how that game in 2012 played out 👇 pic.twitter.com/OhtVx3caCP

This rivalry was forged in different circumstances from most derby confrontations. There is none of the religious divide of Celtic and Rangers, or the politics of Barcelona against Real Madrid, or the spat over title-winning superiority of Manchester United and Liverpool. This is a tale of proximity, an internecine feud.

“There’s no politics, no nationality, nothing like that,” says Nick Hart, who hosts the weekly podcast Achtung! Millwall. “We’re very similar people, from the same backgrounds, same communities. But it’s in the Millwall supporter’s DNA for West Ham to be the ultimate rivals. Nobody else comes into the equation. You’re brought up on this stuff. It’s your history.”

Though possibly more recent history than might be suggested by the two clubs’ early foundations. The hostility that West Ham will face at the Den is no more about dockland rivalry, north-south London disputes or strike-breaking than the animosity when Manchester United visit Anfield is caused by the building of the Manchester Ship Canal.

“It really is about the hooligan era,” says a podcaster who uses the pseudonym Former West Ham Employee on the West Ham Way podcast. “The two clubs had notorious fanbases. And they grated. It came about through vying to be the No 1, battling to see who had the hardest mob. Whenever we’ve played – or even been in close proximity – things have happened.”

Jake Cooper on making the 500th appearance of his career against West Ham today! 👏Watch all the action with NOW! https://t.co/56JOZ0NPsr pic.twitter.com/lTzXOwXhxd

There have only been 18 meetings between these fierce rivals since the Second World War, but absence has certainly not made the heart grow fonder. Here are some of the feud’s most notable flashpoints.

At the 1972 testimonial in honour of Harry Cripps – the renowned Millwall hard man – police horses were sent on to the pitch after West Ham supporters entered the home section at The Den. Fighting spilt over into the streets surrounding the ground.

An even bleaker turn came in 1976, when Millwall fan Ian Pratt died in a skirmish with West Ham fans at New Cross station that led to his fall under a train.

Leaflets were later handed out in the Den’s Cold Blow Lane end with a grainy picture of Pratt and a declaration in capital letters: “A West Ham fan must die next week to avenge him.”

Millwall plundered four goals on Mothering Sunday in 2004 as Tim Cahill’s double helped them to a 4-1 victory over West Ham at the Den in an incident-filled derby.

The hosts missed a penalty and had another saved by Stephen Bywater, who was later sent off. Violence followed in the stands and the match was named “The Mothers’ Day Massacre”.

Mother's Day Massacre ⏮️A 4-1 victory over The Hammers back in 2004. pic.twitter.com/TLi7xkcVJG

A hundred West Ham and Millwall supporters clashed during a screening of England’s 2006 World Cup match against Paraguay in Canada Square, which led to 16 injuries and one hospitalisation.

The clubs’ League Cup meeting in 2009 at Upton Park was listed as Category Five by police, the most serious risk of violence, and resulted in a Millwall supporter being stabbed in Priory Road, near the ground.

The Metropolitan Police said that “planned” scuffles, which involved more than 100 fans, appeared to have been caused by fans without tickets to the game.

Just spotted one Millwall fan outside the ground in blue boxing gloves. He is also wearing what appear to be slippers, so not sure what that means…

Nuno Espirito Santo has only been through the door at West Ham for a matter of months, but he insisted he is fully aware of the significance of today’s fixture.

When asked about his perception of the rivalry, Nuno said: “Since the fixture list came out, this date has been [important], for both of the clubs. It’s special, special game. We look forward to go and compete against a good team.

“It’s a different game from all of the other games, it’s a special game, the atmosphere will be different… Steve [Potts, first-team coach and former West Ham player] has been involved in many of these games, he’s constantly speaking about how special it is for West Ham fans, so we have a lot of information and we are fully aware of the importance of the game.

On potential unrest between fans and the significant police presence, Nuno added: “What we want most is that everything goes well, both fans supporting their teams and no conflict. We have people inside the club who are taking care of that. We have to focus on our tasks.”

The gaffer on tomorrow's fixture ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/6NG6t4t4Fn

#westham on the way to #millwall via #london bridge #whufc #coyi pic.twitter.com/HrWgJ6UtJY

Riot police are very much out in force outside The Den today for the 100th competitive derby between Millwall and West Ham United and first for 14 years. Dog units and mounted officers can been seen patrolling the perimeter of the ground, with 400 personnel deployed to stop violence erupting between rival fans – roughly quadruple the usual number for a fixture here. There has been no sign of any trouble with less than an hour to go before kick-off.

The game has been scheduled for 12.30pm to minimise supporters’ pre-match drinking time, although plenty of fans have been nursing pints before entering the ground. Other measures in place include the use of live facial recognition cameras, while a dispersal order has been imposed covering a large area around the stadium. Police were also planning to escort West Ham fans from South Bermondsey station, which will also be closed to home supporters for up to an hour after full-time. The latter measure has been deemed safer than holding the 1,800 away fans back following the game.

The Millwall-West Ham derby is one of the most notorious in English football and was most recently marred by serious violence when the sides met at Upton Park for a League Cup tie back in 2009. One man was stabbed and the match itself was interrupted on three occasions by fans invading the pitch.

Alex Neil switches out goalkeeper Max Crocombe for Filip Marschall and names the returning Mathis Servais, Kyrell Lisbie and Alfie Doughty on the bench.

Alex Neil names his Lions XI 👊 pic.twitter.com/MP0N9wMatG

Just the one change from the league leaders’ last league match as Kyle Walker-Peters comes in for the injured Joel Veltman.

Today's teamsheet 📋 pic.twitter.com/EmrxYRhsPd

"We have to quiet them down" 🤫West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen is expecting a hostile atmosphere at The Den today 🗣️Watch all the action with NOW! https://t.co/56JOZ0NPsr pic.twitter.com/9tp2225Rq8

The Metropolitan Police will have 400 officers on the streets of east London for this match – about four times the norm for a Championship fixture – and it has enforced a Section 35 dispersal order in the area highlighted on the map below.

A Section 35 order authorises a Police Constable and a Police Community Support Officer in uniform to “exclude a person from an area for a period of up to 48 hours with an Inspector’s authority”.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of the highly anticipated Championship match between Millwall and West Ham United as the two clubs meet officially for the 100th time. This fixture has not been staged since 2012, and the intervening 14 years have done little to temper the ill-feeling between their passionate supporters, who will be anxious to claim bragging rights over their Dockers Derby rivals. The Metropolitan Police have placed a Section 35 dispersal order in the area surrounding The Den and will deploy 400 officers on the streets of east London.

Acrimony between the two clubs has existed since the late 19th century when Millwall Athletic, originally Rovers, battled it out against Thames Ironworks, later renamed West Ham at the Athletic and Memorial Grounds. Sixty of the two clubs’ 99 meetings came between 1899 and 1915, and while they played just seven times between 1946 and 1987, the irregularity of the game only added to its mystique, which has often spilt over into the ugly.

Both head coaches spoke at length about the significance of today’s match, with Alex Neil, in the Millwall dugout, describing it as an encounter that means “absolutely everything” but imploring his players to keep “cool heads”. His counterpart Nuno Espírito Santo revealed that he had been well advised about the game’s importance by Steve Potts, his first-team coach and former West Ham player.

Since the club’s last meeting in 2012, West Ham have ascended into the Premier League, moved into the London Stadium and won the Uefa Conference League, only falling back into England’s second tier last summer where Millwall have remained for all but two seasons. The Lions brushed maddeningly close to promotion in their last campaign as they pushed for an automatic spot until the very last weekend of the regular season before falling to Hull City in the play-off semi-finals.

Much of the pre-match talk will centre on the clubs’ long-standing rivalry, but beneath the bile and belligerence is an intriguing football match between two sides. Millwall are missing 11 first-team players and face the daunting task of stopping a West Ham side who have found their feet in the Championship, scoring 16 goals in their last four league matches.

#1506. It’s fire in Naples!

In Naples, the crisis is now more visible than ever. Traveling to Porto on Wednesday in the Champions League, the Azzurri conceded their seventh defeat of the season in all competitions (4-1), but also displayed worrying nervousness. The image of the heated altercation between Kevin De Bruyne and Lorenzo Lucca at the end of the game illustrated the tensions currently running through the Neapolitan locker room. In the process, Scott McTominay did not hide his annoyance at the situation. “ We have to play better in both areas, we can’t continue like this. We lost 4-1, obviously I’m angry. We have a lot of injuries, but that can’t be an excuse, even if it’s always the same players who come on the pitch. Everyone needs to go home and think about what they can do to improve tomorrow “, explained the Scottish community.

An annoyance which is justified by the worrying sporting situation of the Neapolitan club. Naples is in eighth place in Serie A, is already 14 points behind the leader, Lazio, and is nine points from fourth qualifying place for the C1. On the European scene, Massimiliano Allegri’s squad is the only Italian team not to appear among the top 24. Further proof of the division within the locker room, the exit of Matteo Politano from Sky Italiacriticizing foreign players in particular for not speaking out about the situation. “ Everyone needs to examine their conscience. I put myself forward: I would like others to do it too. Not just us Italians… »

Faced with this critical situation, Massimiliano Allegri is being singled out more than ever. Last night, the transalpine coach did not want to blame his players, mainly citing the lack of solutions on his bench. “ We would have liked to bring in fresh and athletic players, but I only had attackers on the bench. To play matches that require such an expenditure of energy, you have to be able to make changes. Otherwise, we can’t do it, it’s simple. You can only maintain such a rhythm if you have eight or nine changes “. To try to escape this negative spiral, Naples is preparing to carry out a ritiro, according to La Repubblica.

A decision which would have been taken even before the new rout on the Dragão pitch, but which Allegri’s group seems to greatly need. The players should therefore remain together until the reception of Lazio (Sunday, 12:30 p.m.), with the objective of closing ranks and preparing as best as possible for the arrival of the championship leader. Facing the Romans, Massimiliano Allegri himself spoke of a “ final », as the urgency is felt. While the European markets are moving dangerously apart and internal tensions are accumulating, the Italian technician is more threatened than ever. In the event of another defeat, he could leave Napoli, only four months after his arrival.

#1505. How Declan Rice's new role has turned him into the Premier League assist king, saves him from burnout and reduces Arsenal's reliance on set-piece goals

Published: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

For so long, Declan Rice was Mikel Arteta’s lighthouse. ‘You just look at him and you know where to head,’ said the Arsenal boss. ‘A focal point giving clarity and direction to everybody.’

Only, not any more. Arteta had a chat with his midfield general at the start of the season, one Rice described as a ‘really honest conversation’, to discuss how he wanted his role to evolve.

After setting up Kai Havertz’s winner against Liverpool with a superb overlap run and cross on Sunday, Rice revealed what Arteta had told him.

‘I’ve done well but he believes I can still do more and he's drilled that into me,’ said Rice. ‘This season I've really tried to attack that part going forward, trying to come up with assists, create chances, create moments. Being behind the ball as well, linking the play. Being involved with all aspects, for me, is my best position.’

He’s certainly doing the creative part of that assignment. Rice’s assist for Havertz at Anfield was his fifth of the season, the most of any player in the Premier League, and puts him on track to obliterate his previous high of eight in 2023-24. Remarkably, for the corner specialist at the league's renowned set-piece kings, all five have come from open play.

Rice, too, revealed he’d discussed overlapping before the Liverpool game and told Havertz to attack balls into the box. That’s just what they both did.

Arsenal's Declan Rice is top of the assist charts in the Premier League this season with five

His latest came at Anfield on Sunday when he made an overlapping run around Noni Madueke who picks up the ball on the edge of the box...

...Madueke plays the ball into Rice's path and he crosses for Kai Havertz (arm raised) to finish at the back post

In truth, Rice’s role has evolved throughout his time at Arsenal.

In the very early days at the Emirates, Rice spent most of his time sitting in a defensive midfield role.

As the seasons have progressed, especially after Martin Zubimendi’s arrival last summer, Rice has been freed to drive further up the pitch, and occupy that space in the left channel.

You can see from his heat map over his Arsenal career, where the redder zones reflect more touches in that area, how much that role has shifted.

In his first season at Arsenal, Rice pops up all over the pitch...

...the following year he appears as an attacking force on the left side of the pitch...

...as he did again last season alongside Martin Zubimendi when Arsenal went on to win the title...

...but this season he is popping up more on the right-hand side, as seen at Anfield for Havertz's winning goal

What’s most noticeable about this season, following the arrival of Bruno Guimaraes and Arteta’s ability to use converted left back Myles Lewis-Skelly in midfield, is that Rice has now shifted to the right.

That has enabled him to link up more effectively with Bukayo Saka or Noni Madueke on that side.

What is perhaps less obvious, but even more telling, is that despite the sight of Rice bursting into the box on the overlap down the right to set up Havertz, he is actually doing most of his creative work and tempo-setting from deeper on the pitch.

As Rice put it, ‘Being behind the ball as well’.

Early in this campaign, he spent a large portion of games picking up possession between Arsenal's centre backs, allowing the champions to create overloads when building up play and bypass an opposition press.

He’s averaging just one touch in the opposition box per game in the league, the lowest number in any season of his Arsenal career. He’s only played a handful of passes all season beyond the edge of the 18-yard box.

In Arsenal’s victory over Sunderland, in which Rice set up one goal and created another two chances, he was the deepest sitting of all Arteta’s midfielders (No 41)

And yet it’s making him more influential than ever. He’s playing more forward passes than in any season at the club. More passes into the final third, more line-breaking passes. And he's carrying the ball towards goal more frequently than at any point in his Arsenal career.

At the same time, he’s having less defensive responsibility, averaging the fewest ball recoveries and possession wins in the final third of any of his seasons at the club.

There is a small caveat to add here. For as clearly effective and influential as he has been in this evolved role, Rice is still overperforming his numbers a little.

His five assists have come from a total open-play expected assists (xA) tally of just 1.07. No one has overperformed that metric – which measures how likely the chances you’ve created are to result in a goal – as much as Rice.

You only need to look back at a few of those assists this season. His one for Madueke against Nottingham Forest was a simple pass out to the touchline where the winger then did all the work to cut inside and bend a beauty into the far corner.

He did the same for Havertz on the other flank for his equaliser against Chelsea. And it was a little sideways pass to Guimaraes against Sunderland that his midfield partner then whacked into the top corner from long range.

By contrast, Martin Odegaard, for so long his side’s creative hub, is yet to claim an assist from open play despite having an xA of 1.9, the fourth-highest in the division.

But that is not to take away from the superb work Rice is doing. Where he’s really showing his expertise is in how simply he’s making those forward creative passes look. Take these examples:

After his assist at Anfield, Rice creates another chance for Jurrien Timber, poking a little pass that cuts out two Liverpool players to open up space for a long-range shot

Against Everton, he knocks another through the lines into space for Madueke to turn and run on to

And even though Havertz still had everything to do for his goal against Chelsea, Rice’s pass to him takes out four blue shirts

The xA on the above pass might not be high but it creates the opportunity for Havertz to conjure some magic. Short, simple passes that help open up defences.

Rice is doing all this while running less, too. He’s averaging 6.8 miles per game. Over the previous two campaigns, he travelled 7.1.

Perhaps it was always going to have to be this way. It was over the World Cup this summer that the sheer weight of games Rice had played in 2025-26 – 69 for club and country – finally took its toll.

He played through a hamstring injury from Christmas onwards and was substituted early in England’s victory over Croatia with ‘neural pain’ in his back.

'The body's been through a lot this season,’ he said after the semi-final defeat by Argentina. 'I think you can see I'm mentally done, physically done. I need a break now.’

Now, with the likes of Guimaraes and Lewis-Skelly as well as Zubimendi around him, Rice is able to keep starting every game but also do what great midfield metronomes like Rodri and Paul Scholes did before him: control matches without having to bust a gut.

It has allowed Rice to be more selective in his runs forward. Guimaraes, especially, is dynamic enough to sit in for those moments – like at Anfield – when Rice spots the opportunity to make his move.

Rice's movement and backheel allowed space for Bruno Guimaraes to fire in the winning goal against Leeds last month

He did similar against Leeds to set up Guimaraes’ winner, charging into the box to play a neat little backheel to the Brazilian, who fired into the bottom corner.

It allows Arteta, too, to find different ways to open up defences in open play, whether they are sitting deep or pressing man-to-man. Rice is now able to exploit the gaps or pick the locks.

Arsenal have not always had this luxury and, when they frequently struggled to do so in the past, had to turn to set-pieces. Not any more.

Rice may no longer be Arteta's lighthouse but he continues to find new ways to lead Arsenal to glory.

#1504. The Barça group for the Clásico!

FC Barcelona approaches the Clasico against Real Madrid, this Sunday evening at 9 p.m., with several significant absences in its ranks. Coach Hansi Flick will notably have to deal without injured Dani Olmo and Eric Garcia, while Jules Koundé, Andreas Christensen and Roony Bardghji are also unavailable. Despite these packages, the Blaugranas will be able to count on their executives for this shock of the 10th day of La Liga, played at the Camp Nou.

Furthermore, Hansi Flick could offer their first Clasicos in the Blaugrana jersey to several summer recruits, including Anthony Gordon, Karim Adeyemi, Gabriel Jesus, Rodri and Dominik Livaković. Barça, leader of La Liga before this meeting, intends to take advantage of the home advantage to consolidate its position against its great rival Madrid

#1503. Mario Hermoso: “This Roma always wants to win.”

Roma beat Sassuolo 3-0 thanks in part to Mario Hermoso who scored the opening goal.

The Spanish defender spoke to Sky Sport after the game.

“The disappointment in Manchester? When these things happen that you can’t win, football doesn’t leave you thinking. The team wants to win, to stay at the top. For us, it was too important, and we did it.”

“The coach prepares you physically, on the pitch, to find these situations. We go there to make a nice pass or a shot on goal. We continue to work in the same way we work on defense. We do the same to help the attackers score.”

Gasperini’s Roma break scoring record: 31 goals in 11 games

Roma meet with Alejandro Balde’s agent for January

Mancini ruled out vs Sassuolo due to injury

Over 62,000 Roma fans to attend Sassuolo match

Gasperini requests two reinforcements in January

Gollini remains sidelined, Vasquez to replace him

After the match, Nahuel Molina analyzed the game to Sky Sport.
