In brief, for the enumeration of G. huxleyi cells, water samples were pre-filtered using 40-µm cell strainers and immediately analysed with an Eclipse iCyt flow cytometer using ec800 software v1.3.7 (Sony Biotechnology). Calcified G. huxleyi cells were identified as a population of cells with high SSC and high chlorophyll (excitation: 488 nm, emission: 663–737 nm). For the enumeration of intracellular EhV, water samples were pre-filtered through 20-µm filters, and DNA was extracted from 2-µm filters. EhV abundance was determined by quantitative PCR using the major capsid protein (mcp) gene. Absolute abundances were calculated using a calibration curve of DNA at known concentrations.

Planktonic (>0.2 µm and <2 µm) and particle-attached (>20 µm and <200 µm) fractions of the bacterial community were assessed throughout the succession of the induced G. huxleyi bloom in mesocosm bag 7 using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, as previously described24. In brief, water samples were pre-filtered through 200 µm, sequentially filtered through 20-µm, 2-µm and 0.22-µm polycarbonate filters (Isopore, 47 mm; Merck Millipore), and immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen. DNA extraction of the 20-µm and 0.22-µm filters was performed with the DNeasy PowerWater kit (Qiagen), and sequenced following the EMP 16S amplicon protocol targeting the V4 region of the 16S gene using the 515F-806R primers77 including degeneracy to reduce bias towards Thaumarchaeota and SAR1165,66. The particle-attached fraction was sequenced using a paired-end 2× 153 bp Illumina MiniSeq platform at the RUSH Genomics and Microbiome Core Facility. Data analysis for planktonic bacteria was performed using the DADA2 pipeline and ASVs annotated with the RDP classifier. The average sequencing depth per sample and chloroplast read proportion for the planktonic community was previously reported24. Data analysis for particle-attached bacteria was performed using the DADA2 pipeline (setting ‘justConcatenate = TRUE’ to merge the forward and reverse reads introducing 10x ‘N’ in the middle) and ASVs annotated with the SILVA_nr99 reference database. The average sequencing depth for the particle-attached size fraction in bag 7 was 20,734 ± 6,517 (minimum 8,057 and maximum 29,629) reads per sample. Chloroplast reads accounting for 7 ± 8% (minimum 1% and maximum 36%) in the particle-attached fraction were removed. Kruskal–Wallis tests were performed to compare planktonic and particle-attached bacterial fractions for each family and bloom phase (pre-bloom, days 1–6; bloom, days 7–14; and viral infection phase, days 15–23). Pairwise Welch’s t-tests with the Holm–Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons were performed comparing the log2-transformed fold change of particle-attached planktonic bacterial fractions between the bloom phases. For missing samples (day 2 of the planktonic and day 1 of the particle-attached size fraction), the relative abundances were interpolated. Absence of Pseudoalteromonadaceae in some planktonic samples prevented log2 fold change computation.

To prepare cell extracts as chemoattractants, G. huxleyi CCMP 2090 was grown in 19 l modified K/2 medium in 2 carboys with stirring and aeration. One exponentially growing culture (1.2 × 106 cells per ml) was infected with EhV 201 at an MOP of 1:1 while the other culture served as an uninfected control. The viruses were propagated on CCMP 2090, washed and concentrated on 100 kDa Amicon-ultra filters (EMD Millipore), and stored at 4 °C until use within two months. Cells were counted daily using a Multisizer 4 Coulter Counter (Beckman Coulter). After 48 h, the uninfected (4.4 × 106 cells per ml) and infected (0.9 × 106 cells per ml) cultures were filtered onto pre-combusted GF/C filters (47 mm; Whatman) using gentle vacuum (600 mbar under-pressure). Filters were immediately transferred to 500 ml pre-cooled (−20 °C) methanol (HPLC grade, J.T. Baker) and extracted overnight at 4 °C while shaking. Extracts were sonicated for 30 min and filtered through pre-combusted GF/C filters before being evaporated to 20 ml using a Rotovap (30 °C, 70–100 rpm). Extracts were centrifuged at 20,800g for 10 min at 4 °C, and the supernatants were evaporated to complete dryness using a SpeedVac (28 °C, 1,980 rpm). Dried extracts were re-dissolved in methanol to reduce the salt load, aliquoted into eight centrifuge tubes, dried using a SpeedVac, and stored at −80 °C until further use. The dry weight was 57.5 ± 0.3 mg and 38.3 ± 0.5 mg for the uninfected and infected extracts, respectively.

In situ chemotaxis assays (ISCAs) containing the G. huxleyi cell extracts were deployed five times throughout the mesocosm bloom succession, namely at days 3, 9, 12, 18 and 20. For each deployment, 12.5 ml of bloom water were collected per mesocosm bag (1–4; 50 ml in total), mixed and subjected to a quadruple-filtration process. Specifically, the mixed bloom water was first filtered through a 0.2-μm Millex FG (Millipore) to remove large particles, twice through a 0.2-μm Sterivex filter (Millipore), and finally through a 0.02-μm Anatop filter (Whatman). This quadruple filtration aimed to remove all microorganisms from the seawater. We confirmed the efficiency of the filtration procedure using flow cytometry and DNA sequencing78. The filtered bloom water was used as a control in the ISCA and was also used to resuspend the dried G. huxleyi extracts at a final concentration of 1 mg ml−1. The resuspended extracts were filtered through a 0.2-μm Millex FG (Millipore) to remove undissolved particles.

The working concentration of G. huxleyi extracts (1 mg ml−1 of dry weight) is representative of environmental hotspots. Indeed, chemical concentrations decay exponentially with distance away from the ISCA opening (port)41. This means that concentrations sensed by bacteria in the surrounding bloom water will be substantially lower than those in the ISCA wells and within the same order of magnitude as the concentrations arising from the lysis of a phytoplankton cell79.

Treatments (filtered bloom water and the two G. huxleyi cell extracts) were randomly allocated to an ISCA row (consisting of 5 wells with 110 μl each). All wells in a row contained the same treatment, and each treatment was replicated on three different ISCA devices, which were deployed in parallel to act as biological replicates (n = 3). Each ISCA was placed into a flow-damping acrylic enclosure, following a pre-established protocol80. Each enclosure was filled with water coming from the first four mesocosm bags (bags 1–4), previously mixed at equal volume. The flow-damping enclosures were filled slowly with water from the inlet in the lower surface and were sealed with a plug once full. The enclosures were then incubated in situ at 1 m depth for 2 h (ref. 78). Following deployments, enclosures were retrieved and slowly drained. The volume of each ISCA well was retrieved using a sterile 1 ml syringe and 27G needle.

ISCA samples for DNA extraction were snap-frozen immediately. DNA extraction was performed using a microvolume extraction approach (physical lysis method81). Libraries for 16S rRNA gene sequencing were generated for all samples using the Nextera XT DNA Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina) following a previously described protocol for low-input DNA libraries82. Primers targeting the V4–V5 regions of the 16S rRNA gene were used, namely 515F and 926R (CCGYCAATTYMTTTRAGTTT65). Samples were then sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform with a paired-end 2× 300 bp output. Libraries were pooled on an indexed sequencing run and yielded ~300 bp per sample. The composition of the chemotactic bacterial communities was analysed as described above using the DADA2 pipeline, and ASVs were annotated with the SILVA_nr99 reference database. For day 18, a Welch’s ANOVA followed by two-sided pairwise t-tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction were performed to compare the fraction of Alteromonadaceae across chemoattractants using the R ‘stats’ package (v4.5.1; Shapiro–Wilk test and Levene test were performed to assure normality and homogeneity of variances).

To isolate chemotactic bacteria throughout the succession of the induced G. huxleyi bloom, we prepared agar plates made with 0.22-μm-filtered environmental bloom water and amended with 1 mg ml−1 of the corresponding G. huxleyi cell extracts. The agar plates were inoculated with the chemotactic bacterial community from the ISCA wells containing uninfected and virus-infected G. huxleyi extracts and incubated at fjord water temperature (10 °C) until colonies appeared. Individual colonies were then grown in 10% MB in autoclaved seawater overnight at room temperature and at 10 °C. Each isolate went through two additional rounds of purification via successive growth on plates and in liquid cultures. Isolates were identified by 16S rRNA gene Sanger sequencing78. Selected strains (Supplementary Data 1) were further used for genome sequencing and characterization of their chemotaxis towards different G. huxleyi cell extracts.

For genome sequencing, overnight cultures were inoculated in MB medium at 0.1 OD600. Exponentially growing cultures at 1.0 OD600 were centrifuged, and cell pellets of 15–30 mg were re-dissolved in 0.5 ml Zymo DNA/RNA Shield. Genomic DNA extraction and Nanopore sequencing were performed by Plasmidsaurus following their standard bacterial genome sequencing service. Assembled genome sequences were classified at the species level using the GTDB-Tk software toolkit.

For laboratory-based chemotaxis assays, the bacteria were plated from cryostocks on MA. Multiple colonies from each strain were inoculated in 1% MB in artificial seawater (33 g l−1 Instant Ocean, Aquarium Systems) and incubated at 180 rpm and 27 °C for 4 h to promote bacterial motility. An aliquot was fixed with glutaraldehyde (1% final concentration; Sigma Aldrich), stained for 15 min with SYBR Green I (ThermoFisher), and bacterial abundance enumerated using a CytoFLEX S flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter) as described above. Chemotaxis was characterized using ISCA devices that were each loaded with four different 0.2-μm-filtered treatments and incubated at room temperature for 1 h in artificial seawater inoculated with 106 bacteria per ml. As chemoattractants, we used: (1) extract from uninfected G. huxleyi CCMP 2090 cultures (1 mg ml−1 in artificial seawater); (2) extract from virus-infected G. huxleyi CCMP 2090 cultures (1 mg ml−1 in artificial seawater); (3) 10% MB (acting as a positive control), and artificial seawater (acting as a negative control to account for cells entering wells by random motility). Chemoattractants were inoculated in ISCA wells using a sterile 1 ml syringe (Codan Medical ApS) and needle (27 G, BD Microlance). In each ISCA, each row of five wells served as technical replicates for an individual treatment. Each chemoattractant was deployed simultaneously in four ISCA replicates. After incubation, contents of the ISCA wells were recovered using a sterile syringe and needle, technical replicates were pooled80, and 200 µl per sample were fixed, stained and enumerated using flow cytometry. Chemotactic indices (Ic) were determined as ratios of the cell concentrations in treatment wells relative to the average artificial seawater control. For statistical analysis, Ic values were log1p-transformed (ln(1 + x)) and the Levene test of homogeneity of variances and Shapiro–Wilk test of normality were performed using R. All bacteria showed significant differences between the artificial seawater control and the treatments, including the MB control (Dunnett’s test with P < 0.001). Differences between the two cell extracts were assessed using a two-sided Welch’s t-test with the Holm–Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. For fold change comparison, the transformed Ic values were further log2-transformed, the normality per strain and treatment validated using a Shapiro–Wilk test, and treatment differences per strain assessed using a two-sided Welch’s t-test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. The log2-transformed fold changes (LFC) between the infected and control extracts were computed as LFC = mean(log(Inf)) − mean(log(Ctl)) with s.e.m. = √ (VarInf/nInf + VarCtl/nCtl).

Coccolithophore blooms were sampled in the North Atlantic during the NA-VICE cruise in 2012 with large spatial coverage18 and the Tara Breizh cruise in 2019 with high temporal resolution43.

During the NA-VICE cruise, coccolithophore blooms across a 2,000-mile transect between the Azores and Iceland were identified via satellite remote sensing and sampled at 30 stations onboard the RV Knorr between 13 June and 16 July 2012, as previously described18. Samples for DNA extraction and 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing were collected between the surface and 150 m depth with Niskin bottles, and filtered through a 200-μm prefilter onto 0.8-µm polycarbonate filters. Genomic DNA was extracted and amplified in a dual PCR strategy using primers targeting the V1–V3 region of the 16S rRNA gene83 linked to adaptors, namely CS1_27F_YM (ACACTGACGACATGGTTCTACA-AGAGTTTGATYMTGGCTCAG) and CS2_534R_Y (TACGGTAGCAGAGACTTGGTCT-TYACCGCGGCTGCTGG), and subsequently linked to unique sample barcodes for multiplexing. For PCR amplification, the AccuPrime SuperMix II (Life Technologies) was used using the following cycling conditions: denaturation for 5 min at 95 °C, 28 cycles of 30 s at 95 °C, 30 s at 56 °C and 5 min at 68 °C, and final 7 min elongation at 68 °C. The PCR amplicon quality was validated by gel electrophoresis. In a second PCR step, sample barcodes were amplified with the following cycling conditions: 5 min at 95 °C, 8 cycles of 30 s at 95 °C, 30 s at 60 °C and 30 s at 68 °C, and final 7 min elongation at 68 °C. Samples were pooled and purified using AMPure XP beads, and concentrations were estimated using Qubit. Sequencing was performed using a paired-end 2× 300 bp Illumina MiSeq technology at the DNA Services Facility, University of Illinois at Chicago.

During the Tara Breizh cruise, a G. huxleyi bloom patch in the Celtic Sea was identified by satellite remote sensing and sampled onboard the SV Tara between 27 May and 2 June 2019, as previously described21,43. Samples for DNA extraction and sequencing were collected at the maximum turbidity depth (bloom depth) by pumping seawater through a 20-μm prefilter and sequential filtration onto 3-μm and 0.2-μm PC filters. Following DNA extraction, amplicon sequencing of the V4–V5 region of the 16S rRNA gene was performed twice using Illumina MiSeq paired-end 2× 250 bp sequencing technology. Fastq files were obtained from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA: PRJEB50692). Intracellular virus abundances were quantified from DNA extracts of 3-µm filters using droplet digital PCR and specific primers for the mcp gene of EhV. Samples for flow cytometry were collected at the bloom depth with a Niskin bottle and immediately analysed using a BD Accuri C6 Plus Personal Flow Cytometer (BD Biosciences). Cell abundances of calcified G. huxleyi were determined by gating high chlorophyll (excitation: 488 nm; emission: 663–737 nm) and high SSC (488 nm) particles.

All paired-end 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequences were processed using QIIME 284. ASVs were inferred using the DADA2 paired-end denoising workflow, with trimming and truncation parameters adjusted according to amplicon type. For the NA-VICE samples (V1–V3 amplicons), 20 bp were trimmed from the 5′ ends of both forward and reverse reads, leaving 280 bp (forward) and 230 bp (reverse). Only samples that retained at least 10,000 non-chimeric reads after denoising were considered for downstream analysis. Taxonomic assignment was performed on representative sequences from DADA2, using the QIIME 2 classify-sklearn classifier with the SILVA v138 reference database. ASV tables were aggregated to the genus level, and relative abundances were calculated from the full dataset. The Tara Breizh data (V4–V5 amplicons) were analysed using QIIME 2, as previously described43 with the following modifications. After removal of empty reads, the demultiplexed read pairs were repaired using SeqKit285 (v2.3.1). Primer and orientation handling was performed with CutAdapt (v4.2) in two branches per sample, where each branch represents a primer-orientation-specific read set corresponding to one of the two detected amplicon orientations: one in the original R1/R2 orientation and one in the swapped R2/R1 orientation. Reads lacking the primer sequences, that were <75 bp, and had insertions or deletions were removed. For each sequencing run and orientation branch, denoising was done using QIIME 2 DADA2 with pseudo-pooling. Reads were truncated to 215 bp (forward) and 190 bp (reverse) for the first branch, and to 190 bp (forward) and 215 bp (reverse) for the second branch. Before merging, sequences of the second branch were reverse-complemented. ASV identifiers were normalized by sequence content and feature tables merged by summing identical ASV sequences across the sequencing runs and branches. Chimeras were removed using the de novo UCHIME algorithm of vsearch86 (v2.22.1) and non-chimeric ASV counts of the sequencing duplicates were summed. Counts were summed at the ASV level before conversion to relative abundance. Taxonomy was assigned in QIIME 2 using the SILVA v138 99% Naive Bayes classifier. ASV tables were aggregated to the genus level and relative abundance computed. For Fig. 5, a pseudocount of 1 × 10−5 was assigned to samples with relative abundance of exactly ‘0’. A map of the sample locations was created using the cartopy (v0.25.0) package in python (v3.10) with the Natural Earth map data.

To compare relative bacterial abundances from the North Atlantic coccolithophore blooms with diverse oceanic environments, taxonomic profiles from Tara Oceans44 were obtained (https://www.ocean-microbiome.org/). Per sample, relative abundance at the genus and family levels was calculated by dividing read counts for each taxon by the total bacterial and archaeal reads in the corresponding sample. Only samples representing the planktonic bacterial fraction (0.2 to 3 µm and 0.2 to 1.6 µm filter size fraction) were selected. NA-VICE samples were filtered by collection method to keep only cast samples and omit trap samples, while for Tara Breizh all samples labelled as outside the bloom were excluded. Pairwise comparisons of relative abundance distributions were performed at matched taxonomic level and depth range. For the Tara Oceans and NA-VICE comparison, we compared the Alteromonas genus from surface to 150 m depth. Due to limited sequencing depth, which affected our ability to reliably detect Alteromonas, the Tara Oceans and Tara Breizh comparison was performed for the Alteromonadaceae family from surface to 25 m depth. Differences between groups were evaluated using a two-sided Mann–Whitney U test. For Extended Data Fig. 11, a pseudocount of 1 × 10−5 was assigned to samples with relative abundance of exactly ‘0’. A map of the sample locations was created using the cartopy (v0.25.0) package in Python (v3.10) with the Natural Earth map data.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Genome sequences of the isolated bacteria are deposited under NCBI BioProject PRJNA1287515 (BioSample accessions SAMN50000115–SAMN50000135 and SAMN50033443–SAMN50033450; see Supplementary Data 1). 16S rRNA sequences of the tripartite infection with BAM have been deposited in the ENA project PRJEB125234 at EMBL-EBI (run accessions ERR17795793–ERR17795843). 16S rRNA sequences of the particle-attached size fraction of the mesocosm experiment have been deposited under NCBI Bioproject PRJNA694552 (BioSample accessions SAMN64227782-SAMN64227803). 16S rRNA sequences of the ISCA experiments performed during the mesocosm have been deposited in the ENA project PRJEB125099 at EMBL-EBI (run accessions ERR17795618–ERR17795660). 16S rRNA sequences of the NA-VICE cruise have been deposited in the ENA project PRJEB124157 at EMBL-EBI (run accessions ERR17743795–ERR17743899). 16S rRNA sequences used for the comparative analysis of environmental blooms were obtained from https://www.ocean-microbiome.org/ (Tara Oceans samples) and from the ENA project PRJEB50692 (Tara Breizh samples). Flow cytometry data of the mesocosm G. huxleyi bloom has been deposited in Dryad87. Source data are provided with this paper.

Single-cell analysis of viral gene expression during G. huxleyi bloom demise revealed that at most 30% of the population was infected with the virus3,30. The residual cell mortality supporting a synchronized algal bloom demise might be linked to induced pathogenicity within the algal bloom microbiome. To study alga-virus-bacteria interactions, we isolated G. huxleyi, its virus, and the bloom-associated microbiome (BAM) from the G. huxleyi bloom and demise phases. We then followed the dynamics of algal cultures following individual and co-infections with the virus and the BAM. Individual BAM-members were isolated, characterized regarding their enhancement of the algal population demise, and their metabolic niche was evaluated via functional pathway analysis. Created in BioRender; Kuhlisch, C. https://BioRender.com/r4yzhhc (2026).

Algal, bacterial, and viral abundances in xenic cultures of (a) Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, (b) Phaeocystis globosa, (c) Micromonas commoda, and (d-e) Ostreococcus tauri under four conditions: uninfected (circles) and virus-infected (triangles) with (dashed lines) and without (solid lines) antibiotics (Ab). O. tauri was infected with (d) the generalist virus OtV06-12 and (e) the specialist virus OtV5. Arrows indicate antibiotic additions, which were adjusted for each xenic alga to avoid growth-promoting effects and enhance microbiome inhibition. Data are mean ± SD (n = 4 independent cultures for G. huxleyi and n = 3 for all other species). n.d. - not detected, n.s. - not significant, * P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001, **** P < 10−4 (exact P values are provided in the Source data); statistical significance determined by a linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point.

Algal (a), bacterial (b), and viral (c) abundances in axenic cultures of G. huxleyi under four conditions: uninfected (blue) and virus-infected (olive) without (dashed lines) and with (solid lines) inoculation of bacteria. Abundances of G. huxleyi following EhV infection in the presence (yellow) or absence (red) of (a) the bloom-associated microbiome (BAM) and (c, e, g, i, k) of five bacteria isolated from the BAM (see Supplementary Data 1 for strain information). (a) A significantly positive Spearman’s rank correlation was found between the completeness of the fad pathway (KEGG #00071; see Supplementary Data 2 for gene information) and the synergy index of G. huxleyi bloom-derived bacteria (n = 12) isolated either directly from the BAM community (black outline) or from a G. huxleyi bloom (no outline). The blue shaded area represents the 95% confidence interval of the linear regression (blue line). (b) Presence of fad pathway genes in the isolated BAM members (n = 5) and the chemical reactions that the encoded enzymes catalyse. The triacylglycerol (TAG) lipase is not part of the fad pathway but provides initial substrates. Filled boxes indicate the presence of genes, empty boxes indicate their absence. The pink gradient represents SI values, with darker pink representing a higher synergistic effect.

Genus-level composition of (a) the planktonic size fraction (<2 μm and >0.2 μm) and (b) the particle-attached size fraction (<200 μm and >20 μm) of selected bacterial families. The Alteromonadaceae family was dominated by members of the genus Glaciecola, which is highly similar to the genus Alteromonas based on their 16S rRNA gene sequence88. Planktonic Rhodobacteraceae decreased over time and shifted from a high relative abundance in e.g. Amylibacter and Planktomarina to Loktanella and Sulfitobacter, while the particle-attached fraction increased in relative abundance with a dominance in e.g. Planktomarina, Sulfitobacter and Pseudophaeobacter. Both planktonic and particle-attached Pseudoalteromonadaceae decreased over time and consisted solely of Pseudoalteromonas members. Dominant genera are indicated in bold letters in the legend.

Relative abundances of (a) Alteromonadaceae, (c) Rhodobacteraceae, and (e) Pseudoalteromonadaceae in the planktonic (<2 μm and >0.2 μm) and particle-attached size fraction (<200 μm and >20 μm) during the pre-bloom phase (days 1-6), bloom phase of G. huxleyi (days 7-14), and upon viral infection (days 15-23) using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. Log2 fold change (FC) of particle-attached to planktonic occurrences visualizes the particle-association of (b) Alteromonadaceae and (f) Pseudoalteromonadaceae throughout the bloom succession, while (d) Rhodobacteraceae were more abundant in the planktonic size fraction. Statistical significance was determined by Kruskal-Wallis tests (rel. abundances) and pairwise Welch’s t-tests with the Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons (log2 FC), respectively. Boxplots display the median (horizontal line), the interquartile range (IQR; box), and the 1.5 × IQR whiskers (vertical lines). The sample size (n) per bloom phase is indicated.

In situ chemotaxis assays (ISCA) were performed on selected days during the pre-bloom phase (days 1-6), bloom phase of G. huxleyi (days 7-14), and upon viral infection (days 15-23) using two different G. huxleyi extracts, namely cell extracts from uninfected and virus-infected G. huxleyi CCMP 2090 cultures. Filtered seawater was used as a reference. Genus-level composition is shown for (a) Alteromonadaceae that exhibited the strongest chemoattraction to extracts from infected cells during the viral infection phase of the G. huxleyi bloom (days 15-23), (b) Rhodobacteraceae that showed minimal chemoattraction throughout the entire phytoplankton bloom succession, and (c) Pseudoalteromonadaceae that demonstrated the strongest chemoattraction during the pre-bloom and bloom phases.

Boxplots show log1p-transformed chemotactic indices of seven Alteromonas and one Marinomonas strain towards cell extracts from virus-infected (yellow boxplots) and uninfected (green boxplots) G. huxleyi cultures. Bacteria were isolated from ISCA experiments performed during G. huxleyi bloom succession, specifically from wells containing extracts of either uninfected cultures (green label text), virus-infected cultures (yellow label text), or from the same G. huxleyi bloom (grey label text). Agra = A. gracilis, Amac = A. macleodii, Aste = A. stellipolaris, Asp = Alteromonas sp., Msp = Marinomonas sp. (see Supplementary Data 1 for strain information). Boxplots display the median (horizontal line), the interquartile range (IQR; box), and the 1.5 × IQR whiskers (vertical lines) of n = 4 independent ISCA devices. Statistical significance for Alteromonas strains was determined by a two-sided Welch’s t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons (bold text highlights significant comparisons with P < 0.05).

(a) Sample locations at which microbial community metagenomes and metabarcoding data were collected across the global ocean (blue = Tara Oceans) and from coccolithophore blooms in the North Atlantic (orange = NA-VICE, green = Tara Breizh). (b) Comparison of the relative abundance of Alteromonas between surface samples (≤150 m) across the global ocean (Tara Oceans, n = 136) and from coccolithophore blooms (NA-VICE, n = 96). (c) Comparison of the relative abundance of Alteromonadaceae between surface samples (≤25 m) across the global ocean (Tara Oceans, n = 86) and from a coccolithophore bloom (Tara Breizh, n = 20). Statistical significance was determined by a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test.

Uninfected (a, c and e) and virus-infected (b, d and f-i) cultures of axenic G. huxleyi RCC6946 with (b-d) and without (a and e-i) BAM-inoculation were analyzed by flow cytometry. Algal cells (a and b; gate “Cells”) were enumerated by plotting chlorophyll autofluorescence vs. forward scatter (FSC). The gating of algal cells was based on samples from uninfected cultures of each experiment. The bimodal cell distribution in (a) corresponds to calcified and non-calcified subpopulations. Bacteria and viruses (c-f; gates “Bacteria” and “EhV) were enumerated after DNA staining by plotting SYBR Gold fluorescence vs. violet side scatter (vSSC). The gating of bacteria and viruses was based on samples from virus-infected and BAM-inoculated cultures at the end of each experiment. The high-fluorescent particles in (c) are algal cells. The fraction of virus-infected algal cells (g) was quantified using smFISH by plotting the viral probe’s TMR fluorescence (gate “mcp+”). The “mcp+” gate was based on four gates that pre-selected single fluorescent cells using FSC vs. SSC, vSSC area vs. height, and SSC vs. Chlorophyll to reduce non-fluorescent noise. The fraction of dying algal cells (h) was quantified by gating cells with high SYTOX Green fluorescence (gate “SYTOX+”). (i) SYTOX+ cells were further differentiated as being derived from high (dying cells) or low (dead cells) chlorophyll autofluorescent cells. The “SYTOX+” gates were thereby based on three gates that pre-selected singlets (FSC area vs. height), algal cells (FSC vs. SSC), and then optionally chlorophyll autofluorescence (Chlorophyll vs. FSC).

Supplementary Data 1: Bacterial strain summary. Overview of isolated bacterial strains examined for their synergy and benefit during viral infection of G. huxleyi including details of the isolation, genome sequencing, taxonomic annotation, and NCBI accession numbers. Supplementary Data 2: Alignment E-values for proteins assigned to the fatty acid degradation pathway across bacterial isolates. Values represent –log10-transformed minimum E-values. Proteins from each bacterial strain were annotated using eggNOG-mapper (v2.1.13) with the ‘Bacteria’ eggNOG protein database (v5.0) and assigned to KEGG Orthology identifiers associated with the fatty acid degradation (fad) pathway (map00071). Larger values correspond to smaller E-values; ‘inf’ – E-value of 0.0; ‘n.a.’ – no protein assigned. Supplementary Data 3: Composition of modified K/2 medium. Final concentration (in µM) of major nutrients, trace metals, and vitamins of the modified K/2 medium used to maintain G. huxleyi.

#1454. Sublime England thrash Croatia in best performance for a decade

If this is Tuchel-ball, if this is the way Thomas Tuchel wants England to play, then yes, please. More of the same; bring it on. The standard is set.

England’s DNA? This was a total-football annihilation of a top nation. Croatia, 14th in the world and fierce competitors, were cowed and humiliated at home in this Nations League tie. This was the biggest defeat in their proud history – seventh heaven for England, and hell for the hosts.

The visitors were sublime. Harry Kane (twice – 89 goals now for his country), Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon all scored and were outstanding. Bukayo Saka also struck twice. Alex Scott made his first start and will take some dislodging. The Bournemouth midfielder was slick with a snap – perpetual, intelligent, smooth motion.

Harry Kane at the DOUBLE! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿The Three Lions have FIVE in Rijeka 🦁 pic.twitter.com/BRnVXADtHC

Luka Modric has had the most extraordinary career but he was emphatically second best here and was subbed off on 57 minutes at 5-0. He looked bereft, having had Scott and Elliot Anderson run all over him and Mateo Kovacic.

We came out of the World Cup wondering if Tuchel really had an idea of how he can get England over the line. After last Saturday’s defeat by world and European champions Spain, followed by Tuesday’s win over the Czech Republic we still did not know.

But here the standard was set – it was an exhilarating example of the football England are capable of. On display we saw the speed, the movement, the passes under pressure, the ambition, the control and aggression. This was the full package. Bottle it. Bag it. Believe it.

Croatia have an ageing team and are in transition, but they were left looking callow. It looked as though it was men against boys. There were plenty of boys in the stands, with 6,200 children allowed in for what was supposed to be a behind-closed-doors fixture – Croatia’s punishment for crowd trouble.

Their new head coach Slaven Bilic would doubtless have been relieved that the match was not played in front of the usual, passionate, partisan crowd. Even then some of the kids booed and left early. Bilic looked shell-shocked. As well he might.

And Saka makes it FOUR! ⚽️⚽️⚽️⚽️England break to devastating effect - Croatia are reeling... pic.twitter.com/60EgNt4cfh

It was 4-0 at half-time. It could easily have been 7-1 – Kovacic missed a sitter for Croatia at 3-0 and Gordon should have had a hat-trick. How significant is it that England’s three most dangerous players do not play in the Premier League? Probably not very. But the fact they turn out for Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich is. They performed like the top players their clubs think they clearly are.

Gordon heads in to make it THREE! 💥England are cruising 🛳️ pic.twitter.com/nqwUxFmkof

Kane’s commitment was incredible. At one stage Croatia substitute Kristijan Jakić threatened to break clear but was stopped by England’s last man tracking back. It was Kane, one cap short of equalling Peter Shilton’s all-time record of 125 appearances, and it was already 5-0 when that happened.

These could be exciting times for England. Times when they have shaken off the debate over how well or otherwise they did at the World Cup and moved on. Tuchel has talked up that third-place finish; we have tended to dwell on the semi-final exit to Argentina.

And now? If Tuchel does go and win a trophy for England, he will be talking about this game. Previously he referenced the 5-0 demolition of Serbia in Belgrade, during the World Cup qualification. But the Serbians were a rabble. Croatia are not, but were made to look so on Saturday.

Where will this sit among England performances? There was the 2-1 victory away to Italy at the beginning of the Euro 2024 qualification campaign in March 2023. Before that, the 3-2 win away to Spain in 2018, also in the Nations League. But England were more thrilling here. Do we have to go back to 5-1 in Munich in 2001?

The concern will be the familiar England problem of looking like world-beaters in the autumn and worn out by the time a tournament comes around in the summer. But against Croatia there was control and authority as they raised their chances of finishing in the top two and qualifying for next March’s quarter-finals.

The goals rained in – even if the best remained the first as Marc Guéhi intercepted a clearance, Scott took the ball on the half-turn and found Bellingham. He slid it through to Kane who finished high into the net. What a goal.

Bellingham ➡️ Kane! ⚽️The Three Lions lead in Rijeka with their first shot on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/ZLcnGLvj3z

England were swarming all over Croatia. Saka crossed, Gordon took the ball down and turned it back for Bellingham to stab home.

What a touch from Anthony Gordon! 🔥The Barca man squares it to the Real Madrid man and England lead 2-0 ⚽️⚽️ pic.twitter.com/31Y1Ojx44M

Gordon, after twice being denied, got his goal – with another header, as against the Czechs. This time Jarell Quansah, back in ahead of Trent Alexander-Arnold, delivered from the right and Gordon met it to score for the fourth successive game for England. Even before half-time England were not finished as Bellingham crossed low from the left and found Saka, who found the back of the net.

After the break, the hunger remained insatiable. Anderson was sent down the right and Kane slid in. Croatia then lost the ball sloppily inside their own area, Kane thought about shooting but unselfishly fed Saka, who claimed a second goal.

Saka should have had a hat-trick before substitute Morgan Rogers wrapped up the scoring, collecting a ball over the top from the relentless Bellingham – once again captain after Kane went off – and finishing with ease after rounding the goalkeeper. It was a third assist for Bellingham and a seventh goal for England. It could have been double figures.

SEVENTH heaven for England! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿Morgan Rogers is the latest player to put his name on the scoresheet... ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/H5txZRVgLC

Absolutely [that was the 90-minute performance we’ve been looking for]. Maybe three minutes after the three-zero there was a big mistake [Kovacic’s chance] and some easy ball losses but that was a performance of the highest level from everyone. And from the first until the last minute from everyone who started and everyone who came on. Congratulations to the team.

Very, very impressive [to do this] on an away pitch. We created so many chances in the first 40 minutes. We were so fluid from the start. I looked at the clock and thought ‘Oh, this has been a good three minutes, this has been a good seven minutes…’ and it never stopped.

We kept the pace up and played through the gaps, stayed hungry in our counter-pressing and defending.

We played humble and always got the basics right.

Unbelievable from start to finish. We spoke a lot about having a 90-minute game in which we were dominant with and without the ball and that was it out there. We’re at our best when we’re brave and we’re physically overpowering. When we make it a Premier League game and they couldn’t live with our pace, our movement, our runs. And we were clinical.

There’s freedom. All four of us [him, Bellingham, Saka and Gordon] can play in the 10 pocket, play as the nine. I can play as a midfielder. We’re good enough and smart enough so if we lose the ball we can cover in midfield and defence. That’s the way we want to play. It’s so hard for them to pick a man and press. Every man was at the highest level.

Beautiful hotel, lovely weather, we could easily have fallen into that holiday mode. It’s an unusual situation for us. We’ve never been away this long in this kind of camp and that’s the perfect end to the week,

[And now to equal Peter Shilton’s record 125th cap on Tuesday?] That would be nice. That’s why he keeps taking me off, to rest me for the next game. That’s what he said to me after. I’ll be ready to start on Tuesday.

An amazing night for us. We came out from the start on top and played with high energy and we punished them.

It was special and fun to play. We were really clinical today. Two goals for England is always a nice feeling.

We showed the hunger, passion and quality we had. A mixture of everything we wanted to show.

[Bellingham] was amazing tonight. He deserved man of the match and deserves to be player of the year.

At least the Croatia fans did not seem too dispirited, the kids smiling and waving at the camera, despite the utter trouncing their team took.

England were terrific but how much of that was because Croatia were terrible will be open to debate.

Eze just overcooks the pass that would have released Gibbs-White to run through on goal.

That was Bellingham’s third assist and should it stay 7-0 after two minutes of stoppage time, it will be Croatia’s heaviest defeat.

Nice line from the englandstats.com X account - who said you can’t win anything with kids… watching. Although quite a lot of them have now headed for the exits. This has been remarkable.

Croatia 0 England 7 (Rogers) He barely celebrates but it was a finish off the highest class. He bent his run to make Jakic play him onside, ran down the left when through one-on-one, feigned to cut in then rounded the keeper on the outside to shoot crisply into the open net as Livakovic, who has not been at fault all night, scrambled desperately.

SEVENTH heaven for England! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿Morgan Rogers is the latest player to put his name on the scoresheet... ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/H5txZRVgLC

Rogers is fouled but not before he pings a pass out to Saka on the right. The Arsenal winger darts at Perisic then fizzes a pass across the box to Bellingham who almost trips over himself when block-tackled.

Quansah blocks Perisic’s cross and Croatia want a penalty for Konsa’s tackle on Ivanovic. Looked OK to me and the referee.

Lewis-Skelly → HallGibbs-White → Anderson.

So no Alexander-Arnold or Calvert-Lewin. I suspect he never really intends to give either a decent number of minutes unless forced by circumstances.

England are readying two more substitutes. England scored six against France only a couple of games ago, can they go one better? They put seven past North Macedonia in 2023 but Croatia are two levels above that side.

Bellingham and Eze are playing through the middle now with Rogers down the left.

England really ought to be in double figures by now.

Saka spurns a chance for his hat-trick at the back post when teed up with a Rogers cross from the left.

Croatia 0 England 6 (Saka) Frankly ridiculous. Stanisic, in the right-back position, chips the ball with his left foot across the penalty area straight to Saka who chests it down, plays a one-two with Kane and then buries a right-foot shot past the utterly exposed Livakovic. I know Stanisic and Kane are team-mates at Bayern but that is taking comradely generosity to preposterous extremes.

It's a GIFT for England! 🎁🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿Bukayo Saka has his second... The Three Lions are relentless. pic.twitter.com/33a8oxd3be

Gordon hares down the left at full pelt, the ball seemingly velcroed to his left foot as he makes the byline and cuts the ball back looking for Kane. Vuskovic makes the first block that rebounds to the winger and Gvardiol the second.

Kane’s wandering is often a source of frustration but he has been superb tonight even if he has been allowed to run free.

Pickford catches the corner at his front post. England go forward, pulling defence and midfield one way and then the other with their incisive passing.

Croatia have a corner. Matanovic’s shot from 20 yards takes a deflection and dribbles wide.

Vuskovic has been very impressive for Brighton and Guradiola felt Gvardiol was worth his weight in gold. They have been rubbish tonight.

Bellingham now has the chance of doubling up when Pasalic carelessly loses the ball and turns in horror to see Gordon striding away with it. The Barcelona winger looks for Bellingham and finds him with a cute pass down the inside left. Bellingham stops in the hope Livakovic will go down but when he tries to dink it over him he skews it past the right post.

Croatia 0 England 5 (Kane) That brief revival of Croatia’s press dies a death as England waltz through the midfield again and Anderson drives into the box down the right and bends a cross around the retreating centre-backs to the back post. Kane slides in to prod it home, telescoping out his right leg to convert with the outside of his boot.

Harry Kane at the DOUBLE! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿The Three Lions have FIVE in Rijeka 🦁 pic.twitter.com/BRnVXADtHC

Bellingham pings a diagonal out to Gordon who dribbles into the box down the left, executes a step-over to gull the right-back and then cuts the ball into the six-yard box. Gvardiol wellies it away from Bellingham.

England sweep the ball around confidently with Kane sitting deep and spraying some passes out to the wings with precision.

Ivanovic times the press perfectly with Modric to dispossess  Saka and then slip the ball ahead to Mantanovic and the Freiburg forward tries to catch Pickford napping with an early shot from 30 yards that whistles past the left post. It did give Pickford the hurry-up.

Matanovic is penalised for a foul on Konsa which didn’t look like a foul to me.

The young crowd’s verve has been thoroughly doused by that first-half performance and you can hear the England fans at the start of the half as Croatia kick off.

Matanovic → MusaVlasic → BaturinaMario Pasalic → Sucic

“He’s like a grown man playing against children, giving them a pat on the head as he goes past them.”

England have been magnificent going forward and with their press. Croatia have been shambolic. Bilic lasted six years in his first stint in the job. He’ll be lucky to last six months in this spell if this is the level of his players’ commitment.

Racking my brains to recall the last time England played this well against a leading nation, against any nation in fact. Maybe it was the 3-2 win away over Spain, again in the Nations League in 2018?

Croatia 0 England 4 (Saka) It’s as if Croatia have thrown in the towel. They let Gordon run in behind again on the left and pass to Bellingham who faces up Modric, jinks to his left, shimmies with a wiggle of the shoulder to beat him down the side and then centre to Saka who taps it in, left alone by the negligent Vuskovic and Gvardiol.

And Saka makes it FOUR! ⚽️⚽️⚽️⚽️England break to devastating effect - Croatia are reeling... pic.twitter.com/60EgNt4cfh

Blimey! Kovacic has just missed an open goal as he exploited a lack of concentration at the back by Anderson to blindside him and take the ball off him to dribble to his right through the box with Pickford scrambling like crazy. Once he had opened up the gap to shoot through from the right of the penalty spot, he speared it inches wide. The crowd could not be more deflated if you poked them with a hat-pin.

A STUNNING miss from Mateo Kovačić 🫣The Man City man rounds the keeper and misses an open goal. pic.twitter.com/YfPuDehwYf

I wonder if Luka Modric has ever been in the position where he has not been the best player on the pitch in a headband? Well tonight he’s not, as Alex Scott has been excellent on his first England start. He’s pressed high, dropped deep, won the ball back, beaten his man. It’s just amazing it’s taken Tuchel this long to start him.

I think a few of us (me included) might have thought Trent Alexander-Arnold was the only England full-back who could have provided the cross for Gordon to score against the Czech Republic. Well we were wrong, as Quansah produced a carbon copy of Trent’s cross for Gordon to score with his head against Croatia. Who knew he had that in his locker?

Croatia 0 England 3 (Gordon) His goal on Tuesday was a very rare header and now he’s added a second. Kane sent Quansah down the right and the right-back whipped over a cross that Gordon allowed to bounce in front of him and then flopped rather than dived forward to bury at the back post. He’s the new Nat Lofthouse.

Gordon heads in to make it THREE! 💥England are cruising 🛳️ pic.twitter.com/nqwUxFmkof

A spell of possession beyond 30 seconds for Croatia for the first time. Scott is in the right place to intercept and scupper the first thrust and then Pickford comes a long way off his line and has a bit of a flap at a cross but gets enough of his fist on it, even if he misjudged the flight, to get away with it.

Bilic has sent his outfield subs to warm up. Might be some damage limitation imminent. Modric, if he is to play, ought to be as a 10 not in this deep role.

The young locals are growing restless now. Bood greeted England’s second goal and it felt they were directed at Croatia, rather than the England team. England’s 100-strong band of supporters are making themselves heard and are witnessing an excellent performance so far.

Thomas Tuchel could not believe Anthony Gordon did not kill the game from Bellingham’s cross. He turned to the bench when the ball did not hit the back of the net and angrily remonstrated about the fact England had not scored. He wants this game done and dusted while his team are so dominant.

The tide is relentless. Konsa miscues Saka’s cross from a  free-kick behind for a goal-kick and moments later Anderson, flooding into acres of vacated space, blazes over from 20 yards.

England are playing with the fluency and swagger of a side that are 5-0 up. In fact they could well have been. Kane’s goal was his 88th for England. Bellingham’s his 14th.

Bellingham quickly returns the favour to Gordon with a brilliant run down the right. Gordon checks his run then bends it past Vuskovic’s shoulder to receive the curling cross but he clips it from six yards straight into Livakovic’s chest as the goalkeeper spread himself starfish style.

Croatia 0 England 2 (Bellingham) A Clásico goal. Saka’s cross from the right, looking for Kane again, is overhit. But Gordon is there to trap it on the volley, take it down then slip a clever pass to Bellingham who pokes it past Livakovic. England are off to a flyer. Barcelona assist → Real Madrid finish.

What a touch from Anthony Gordon! 🔥The Barca man squares it to the Real Madrid man and England lead 2-0 ⚽️⚽️ pic.twitter.com/31Y1Ojx44M

England tear a hole through the heart of the Croatia defence again. Modric and Kovacic are just being swamped. Gordon, who was on the underlap as Hall brought it forward, pings the pass from the middle out to Saka who faces up Perisic and whips an inswinging cross with his left to the back post that Vuskovic juts gets to before Kane to glance it behind.

This is seriously the best I have seen England move the ball in a very long time. Their passing is slick and quick and they are so dangerous. Alex Scott is making a real difference in midfield. Feels strange it has taken Thomas Tuchel until now to start him but he is making a real impression and played a clever part in Harry Kane’s excellent team goal.

Another heart-in-mouth moment for the Croatia defence when Kane, drifting out to the right, arrows in the perfect cross that sits up nicely for Saka to toe towards goal from close range. It dribbles past the post and the flag goes up to spare his recriminations.

England have started this game brilliantly, but Croatia have been woeful. They’ve barely strung a pass together and should be two goals down already.

England almost make it two in two minutes when their high press, vigorously applied, forces another error and allows Anderson tos end Gordon racing behind Stanisic down the left. Saka keeps pace with him through the middle but Gordon, in the form of his life, is never going to lay it off and hammers a shot instead that Livakovic turns away.

And that is exactly why it pays to warm-up seriously. Kane was lethal in the pre-match warm-up, see my earlier post, and finished his first chance in the game superbly. Practice makes perfect.

Croatia 0 England 1 (Kane) Gvardiol brings the ball out of the area to the left then sprays a pass into the centre-circle that his City team-mate, Guehi, intercepts. Guehi passes it to Scott who shifts it quickly upfield to Bellingham and the No10 slips a delightful reverse pass between the left-back and centre-half into Kane’s path. The England captain calmly lifts his shot over Livakovic and high into the net.

Bellingham ➡️ Kane! ⚽️The Three Lions lead in Rijeka with their first shot on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/ZLcnGLvj3z

Sucic is penalised for a sliding tackle on Bellingham that legs up the England forward in full flight down the left. Saka takes it, crossing on a shallow arc to the 18-yard line. Guéhi cushions a header but too close to a defender for Kane to pounce.

Anderson takes the corner short and Croatia defend the belated cross.

Looks like the Croatian kids were busy in art and English classed this week, as they unfurled a banner that read ‘It’s not coming home’ in one side of the ground as the game kicked off.

England attack up the left patiently, turning back when necessary. Kane drops deep and fires a pass to Bellingham who plays it down the inside-left for Gordon who runs beyond Vuskovic and rakes a left-foot shot that Livakovic, his Cam Nou team-mate, turns behind.

Alex Scott is given the first kick of the game, knocks it all the way back to Pickford who pumps it so long that Livakovic comes for it and makes a mess of it, shanking it out for a throw-in.

The Croatia national anthem is belted out. Croatia are heart-clutchers when they sing their anthem. It seems an increasingly common practice.

And it does sound like a schoolboy international. England are in red shirts and navy shorts, Croatia in their white and red chequerboard.

You can hear the players singing the national anthem.

Three sides of the ground are now full of small children – and some bigger children who look suspiciously like adults. There’s every chance that I either end this game with a headache or running away from a pack of dogs, given the high-pitched home support.

I just watched Anthony Barry put on a finishing drill with some of the England players. The standard was pretty high, but the quality of Kane’s finishing was, unsurprisingly, superb. He scored with seven of his eight shots past James Trafford and Jason Steele. The one shot he didn’t score with forced Steele into an excellent save. You often see players go through the motions in the pre-match warm-up, but not Kane. He hit every shot like he was trying to win the game in the 90th minute. England’s starters have now gone in ahead of kick-off.

[The camp] has been very good, helped us unwind and recharge the batteries after two intense matches. We have been on the road for a few days, the setting was beautiful. Now we need to switch on which is very difficult [because] the atmosphere is very different with 6,000 children in the stadium. We want to make it a really competitive game but the surrounding is very different. I think wee are up for it.

[Alex Scott] did so well in training and did so well when he made his debut so he brings the full package. He has legs, good at defending, good in the high press, smooth on the ball and good decision-making. That is why he has our trust.

It was a close decision [over Alexander-Arnold] but we decided for Jarrell to start. We will have a lot to defend especially on that side with Perisic and Jarrell did well with Bukayo. We have Trent as an option from the bench.

We need a complete performance in all aspects, adapt to the circumstances. Our physicality, if it is a real competitive match then we would have the edge. Now it feels more like an open training session with the environment and that will suit them better.

But I hope we can bring the intensity and then have the edge.

"To be fair, I don't care" 🤷‍♂️😂Never change, Slaven Bilić 🇭🇷 pic.twitter.com/hBrtZ5TiBy

Loud (high-pitched) cheers for the Croatia team from children inside the Rijeka Stadium. Luka Modric, aged 41, is starting for the home team. He’s a year older than Wayne Rooney, who retired from international football nine years ago. The England players were booed when they entered the pitch. These kids know what they are doing.

I was here eight years ago when it really was a behind-closed-doors game for England. This is very different. There are around 6,000 Croatian children, with their guardians, here and the stands are filling up. It’s also pretty noisy with all the pre-match music.

In 2018, we could hear exactly what the managers and players were shouting – Jordan Henderson was particularly loud – but I don’t think that will be the case this time around. The noise from the fans may be quite high pitched today, but I don’t think it will be quiet at all.

England have 100 fans here and, mercifully, they have not been forced to watch from inside the metal caged away end. They haven’t been allowed to bring in England flags, so it’s currently quite hard to locate exactly where they are.

Croatia Livakovic; Stanisic, Vuskovic, Gvardiol, Perisic; Modric, Kovacic; Ivanovic, P Sucic, Baturina; Musa.Substitutes Pandur, Kotarski, Smolcic, Sutalo, Kramaric, Vlasic, Mario Pasalic, Jakic, Marco Pasalic, Matanovic, Luka Sucic, Misic.

England Pickford; Quansah, Konsa, Guéhi, Hall; Anderson, Scott; Saka, Bellingham, Gordon; Kane.Substitutes Trafford, Steele, Alexander-Arnold, Chalobah, Ngumoha, Branthwaite, Lewis-Skelly, Rogers, Garner, Calvert-Lewin, Gibbs-White, Eze.

Thomas Tuchel was glowing about Alex Scott in his pre-match media duties ahead of today’s game against Croatia and the midfielder has been handed his first England start.

Scott has come in for Myles Lewis-Skelly in what looks to be an attacking change from Tuchel, the England head coach.

Tuchel had taken Scott to the United States on his pre-World Cup training camp, but the Bournemouth midfielder was not part of the squad for the tournament-proper.

On Scott, Tuchel said: “I am super impressed by Alex Scott, I think he is at the moment one of the best central midfielders in the Premier League and he just proves it in every training session. He had a fantastic debut the other day and really really impressed me.”

🇭🇷🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Croatia's starting XI vs. England!Petar Musa and Martin Baturina get their first starts under Slaven Bilić! pic.twitter.com/dPt32fiXbh

Your #ThreeLions for Saturday night 🔴🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 pic.twitter.com/A2M4lMfBNj

Jordan Pickford has revealed he spends up to three hours talking to a “mindwork coach”.

The England goalkeeper has worked with sports psychologists for some time but has gone into detail about how committed he is as he faces a challenge to his No 1 spot from James Trafford.

Pickford will start for England in the Nations League tie against Croatia, and next Tuesday’s fixture at home to the Czech Republic, having missed out on the past two games.

Trafford was in goal for the 3-2 loss to Spain and the 2-0 victory away to the Czechs and although Thomas Tuchel has said Pickford remains his first choice it is known that he and his coaching staff are huge admirers of Leeds United’s new goalkeeper.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is expected to drop back down to the substitutes’ bench for England’s third Nations League game against Croatia in Rijeka.

Despite Alexander-Arnold providing an assist for Anthony Gordon against the Czech Republic, England head coach Thomas Tuchel is expected to replace him with Jarell Quansah at right-back.

Jude Bellingham is also in line for a recall, most likely in place of Morgan Rogers, while Tuchel had been hopeful of Ezri Konsa returning to fitness to replace Trevoh Chalobah in the centre of defence. Goalkeeper Jordan Pickford replaces James Trafford.

Uefa fined the Croatian football federation £80,000 and ordered them to play their next Uefa-sanctioned home match behind closed doors because of their fans’ racist chanting and for fireworks offences during a Nations League match against France in 2025. Croatia have played Fifa-sanctioned World Cup qualifiers and friendlies at home in front of fans since but tonight is the first in Uefa competition and hence the ban.

However, a caveat in Uefa’s disciplinary regulations allows the home federation in such circumstances to fill the ground to 75 per cent of its capacity with “children up to the age of 14 (duly accompanied) from schools and/or football academies invited to the match free of charge”. And given the scrum outside the stadium this afternoon, that is what is happening.

Advertisement | GambleAware | 18+ Betting on the football tonight? Take a look at these tips and offers chosen by Telegraph Media Group

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of England’s Uefa Nations League Group A3 match against Croatia in Rijeka. Matches between the two are relatively frequent – 12 in 30 years. Croatia have beaten England three times in the 10 competitive meetings, home and away in qualification for Euro 2008, which dealt the England manager a blow from which he could not recover, and the World Cup semi-final in Moscow in 2018.

The extraordinary thing about both the first two defeats – the ‘Wally with the Brolly’ match in November 2007, Steve McLaren’s last in charge, and the home tie on October 10 2006 – is that Luka Modric played in both. And now eight days shy of 20 years since his first appearance against England, he is still running their midfield at the age of 41.

England have had the upper hand since Russia, winning in the Nations League at Wembley in 2018, opening their Euro 2020 campaign with a 1-0 victory by virtue of Raheem Sterling’s goal and then in June when they were at their fluent best, a rare occurrence, in the second half of their first World Cup group game to push on from 2-2 to finish 4-2.

Slaven Bilic, manager from 2006-12, is back in charge for his second spell but his squad still relies heavily on experienced players. Modric is the eldest but is joined by greybeard stalwarts Ivan Perisic, Ante Budimir and Andrej Kramaric, both 35. Spain hammered them 4-1 in midweek after they had started with a 2-1 victory over Czech Republic in Prague.

England, who rattled Spain and should have gone 3-1 up but lost 3-2, were much better in the second half in Prague against a team reduced to 10 men and deserved their 2-0 win, have played at the tiny Stadion Rujevica (capacity 8,279) once before, drawing 0-0 in 2018.

Thomas Tuchel, who changed three of his back four on Tuesday, may stick with Lewis Hall after he made a positive impression in combination with Anthony Gordon. As for Trent Alexander-Arnold, who set up the first goal, Tuchel does not go out of his way to undermine the perception that for all his unique quality, he just doesn’t fancy the Real Madrid right-back at all.

It’s up to Alexander-Arnold to make a compelling case if picked today or at Wembley on Tuesday to persuade the German head coach not to restore his beloved if brittle ‘Reecey’ James at the first opportunity.

#1453. Meet Brighton's merry band of unlikely heroes: a midfielder taking tips from Lionel Messi, a twinkle-toed son of a ballerina and the £3m bargain now running the Premier League

Published: 02:00 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 02:00 EDT, 6 November 2026

Noel Gallagher arrived at the Etihad Stadium at the weekend hoping to witness a repeat of his beloved Manchester City's FA Cup triumph, only to be sent packing to the soundtrack of the High Flying Seagulls.

That has been the story – no, not morning glory – of Brighton's season. Fabian Hurzeler's side sit third and are beginning to build a compelling case as the Premier League's most unexpected title challengers since Leicester City's remarkable triumph a decade ago.

Even Danny Murphy, rarely one for lavish praise, was impressed by what he saw after the City win.

'They are such a smart team and they are an absolute pleasure to watch with the ball,' he said on BBC's Match of the Day. 'They are brave. They find a way. They are tactically very good.

'No worries who they are playing. There's no respect. They were willing to risk losing to win and that is what you want.'

Brighton's squad is packed with a number of unknowns, courtesy of a scouting network that has been unearthing gems from across the globe for years. This time, though, with an energetic, charismatic coach in Hurzeler and a perfect blend of youth and experience, there is a growing sense that all the pieces may be coming together at exactly the right moment.

Here, Daily Mail Sport's football reporter Tara Anson-Walsh takes a look at the players driving Brighton's unlikely title charge and the stories behind how they ended up on the south coast...

Brighton's squad remains packed with a number of unknowns, courtesy of a scouting network that has been unearthing gems from across the globe for years

With an energetic, charismatic coach in Hurzeler and a perfect blend of youth and experience, there is a growing sense that all the pieces may be coming together at the right moment

A central tenet of Brighton's success this season, 24-year-old Verbruggen has six clean sheets in the Premier League, the joint-most alongside Arsenal's David Raya.

The Dutchman began his career with hometown club NAC Breda before moving to Belgium in 2020. Admired by former Seagulls boss Roberto De Zerbi for his ability to play out from the back, 6ft 4in Verbruggen arrived in England in 2023 for £16.3million, a Belgian league record fee for a goalkeeper.

Three years on, the player who grew up idolising Edwin van der Sar is unsurprisingly being mooted by Real Madrid as a potential long-term replacement for Thibaut Courtois, while Bayern Munich and Tottenham also retain an interest.

Verbruggen has six clean sheets in the Premier League, the joint-most alongside David Raya

The twinkle-toed 27-year-old owes his deft feet to his mother, a professional ballerina who travelled the world performing, as well as to a childhood spent playing tennis in the Netherlands.

After a difficult initial transition from the Eredivisie to Turkey in 2018, the arrival of Vitor Pereira at Fenerbahce in 2021 and a move to wing-back proved the catalyst for Kadioglu's rapid rise.

Brighton regarded the Turkey international's versatility as a key asset. Capable of operating at either full-back position or in midfield, he joined for £25m in the summer of 2024 after impressing at the Euros as one of Hurzeler's first defensive signings.

Kadioglu owes his deft feet to his mother, a professional ballerina who travelled the world performing, as well as to a childhood spent playing tennis in the Netherlands

For a 19-year-old, Vuskovic has already seen his fair share of the world, gaining experience in Poland, Belgium and Germany after emerging as one of Croatia's brightest talents at Hajduk Split.

After becoming the youngest-ever player to feature in the Croatian top flight, the then 16-year-old was snapped up by Tottenham in 2023 and sent out immediately on loan to Hamburg when he joined the north London club two years later.

There, Vuskovic enhanced his reputation as a robust defender, aerial threat and aggressive presser. Brighton subsequently opted to break the bank, paying a club-record £50m and offering the promise of first-team football to secure his signature.

Brighton paid a club-record £50m to Tottenham for 19-year-old centre back Vuskovic's services, sealing the deal with the promise of first-team football

Brighton through and through, Dunk joined the club from Wimbledon's academy aged 12 and has gone on to make 531 appearances under nine managers before being rewarded with the captain's armband in 2019.

Born in the city to a father who played non-League football in Sussex, Dunk has been the one constant throughout Brighton's rise from League One to Europe. Unfazed both on and off the pitch, there is a running joke in the Dunk family that he doesn't reply to his text messages for five days.

Now entering the twilight of his career, Dunk remains the embodiment of the club's modern success, while Hurzeler relies on his influence to remind the younger players of its humble beginnings.

Dunk has been the one constant throughout Brighton's rise from League One to Europe since joining from Wimbledon aged 12

The France youth international grew up among the sports cars and yachts of Monte Carlo and broke through at nearby Nice before signing for PSV Eindhoven in 2019.

Admired within Brighton's headquarters for his versatility, particularly his ability to play across the back line, Boscagli was a long-term target. Despite not being the tallest defender at 5ft 11in, his impressive spring gives him a strong aerial success rate, while his comfort on the ball was another attribute the Seagulls coveted. Brighton tested PSV Eindhoven's resolve across multiple transfer windows before finally landing their man on a free transfer last year.

After a rocky first season largely spent on the bench last term under Hurzeler, Boscagli spent this summer doing the hard yards, checking in for pre-season already at, in his words, 'close to 100 per cent fitness', a trick which has certainly paid off. Moved from centre back to left-back this season, Boscagli has since appeared in every game.

Admired within Brighton's headquarters for his versatility, particularly his ability to play across the back line, Boscagli was a long-term target

It is no coincidence that Brighton's title charge has coincided with Pascal Gross's dazzling return from an 18-month stint at his boyhood club Borussia Dortmund in January. Ageing 'like a fine wine', Hurzeler recently said of the 35-year-old.

Gross has quite literally run the show this season, covering the most distance of any Premier League player, running 107.4km across the opening nine games.

A little-heralded German from Ingolstadt, Gross caught the eye of the Seagulls after managing to record more chances than any other player in the Bundesliga in the 2016-17 season despite his side getting relegated, and became the Seagulls' first-ever Premier League signing at £3m.

Despite the youth of their manager, Brighton have long prized the importance of experienced players, and Gross has brought this in abundance back to the south coast.

Gross has quite literally run the show this season, covering the most distance of any Premier League player, running 107.4km across the opening nine games

The Mali-born midfielder was plucked out of obscurity by Gothenburg two years ago, bringing him in from Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, the club where former Manchester City icon Yaya Toure began his career.

Two years and a small sample size of just 15 senior appearances later, Brighton deployed their similarly talented scouting methods to bring Yalcouye to the Premier League. An immediate loan to Sturm Graz ensued, where he ended the season as the Bundesliga Young Player of the Year after being deployed as a box-to-box midfielder, a defensive midfielder and an out-and-out winger down both flanks.

This was followed by a disappointing campaign at Swansea last term, where he started just ten Championship matches as a holding midfielder.

Injuries to key players this season have seen Yalcouye thrust into the No10 role for the first time, and it appears Hurzeler may have accidentally stumbled upon a winning formula, with the 20-year-old recording three goals in 15 appearances in all competitions and emerging as one of Brighton's standout performers so far this season.

The 20-year-old has recorded three goals in 15 appearances in all competitions and emerging as one of Brighton's standout performers so far this season

The Paraguay midfielder joined as a 21-year-old from Lionel Messi's Inter Miami last January and hasn't looked back, notching ten goals and one assist in his first full season at the club.

'He always told me to play forward and, when I have the ball, to have no fear,' Gomez said of the Argentine in an interview soon after joining, a sentiment which clearly resonated as he proceeded to shoot, and score, from the halfway line against Crystal Palace last month.

Gomez, who broke through the ranks at Libertad in 2022, was admired for his impressive stamina as well as his physicality, an asset which Brighton felt would help him transition well into the Premier League.

Able to cover large areas of the pitch while remaining aggressive in pressing and duels, Brighton have been left clearly satisfied with the reported MLS record £11m they paid for him, and which will undoubtedly skyrocket amid reports he is drawing admirers from AC Milan and Atletico Madrid.

The Paraguay midfielder joined as a 21-year-old from Lionel Messi's Inter Miami last January and hasn't looked back, notching ten goals and one assist in his first full season at the club

Born into a footballing family, Ayari's Tunisian father travelled to Sweden to become a footballer in his youth, and although this wasn't a success, his dream transferred to his two sons, with Ayari's younger brother plying his trade at AIK, in the Swedish top flight.

It was while a 21-year-old Yasin was also at AIK that he was spotted by Brighton's technical team, who admired his versatility and technical skill, traits which have been honed by Brighton's attack-minded, possession-based style of play.

The £3.5m signing spent a difficult first full season on loan in the Championship split across Coventry and Blackburn, although Ayari now credits that period for developing his mental resilience as he was handed a fresh start following the arrival of Hurzeler.

The £3.5m signing spent a difficult first full season on loan in the Championship at Coventry and Blackburn, although Ayari now credits that period for developing his mental resilience

Defensive frailties last season at left back, the position he had been signed to play in, meant that Maxim De Cuyper slipped down the pecking order at the Amex and saw his game time limited.

Yet injuries to wingers Yankuba Minteh and Kaoru Mitoma have seen the 25-year-old grasp an opportunity to play higher up the pitch with both hands, recording four goals and four assists in 14 appearances.

Developed through his childhood side Club Brugge's academy, De Cuyper played as a winger until he was 14, and his form in that position this season will certainly be giving Hurzeler something to think about when his two explosive wingers return from injury.

Yet injuries to wingers Yankuba Minteh and Kaoru Mitoma have seen the 25-year-old grasp an opportunity to play higher up the pitch with both hands

The then 18-year-old was signed last summer for £31.4m, Brighton's fourth-most expensive signing and a hefty investment in a teenager who had spent just one season in senior football.

But the Seagulls were investing in potential, and Kostoulas had just enjoyed an impressive breakthrough season at the club he had been at since he was 12, Olympiakos, scoring seven league goals - including one in the play-offs - as the Athens side won the Greek Super League.

Recognised for his ability to play in all positions across the front line, Kostoulas was admired by Brighton for his technical skill in linking play, beating defenders, as well as boasting the physicality of a player beyond his years.

He has already surpassed last season's tally of two goals with three, plus a further three assists, in his opening nine appearances in the Premier League, and Brighton fans will be anticipating much more to come from this exciting youngster.

#1452. Sydney FC fans vow to return to the stands after ugly clash with police sparked calls for boycott

Published: 01:23 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 03:07 EDT, 6 November 2026

Sydney FC's active supporter group The Cove will return to the stands for the first time since October's derby, following a bitter dispute over allegations police assaulted a teenage fan and handcuffed supporter leaders before throwing them out.

The group will be back for Friday night’s match against Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park, Sydney, after talks involving the club, NSW Police, Venues NSW and stadium security.

The Cove had threatened to boycott matches after the October 16 derby with Western Sydney Wanderers, accusing police of the 'worst policing standards' in the fixture’s 14-year history and demanding the club defend its fans.

Its return comes amid a broader push for reform, with Football Supporters Association Australia declaring that repeated reviews and weekly discussions with police are no longer sufficient.

The dispute followed a scoreless derby attended by more than 30,000 spectators at Allianz Stadium.

The Cove alleged a 17-year-old supporter was repeatedly slammed into safe-standing rails by police before being struck in the back of the head.

Sydney FC supporter group The Cove will return to Allianz Stadium following a bitter dispute over policing at October's derby

It also claimed two chant leaders, known as capos, were removed from the stadium, while five members of its leadership were handcuffed, pressed against walls and ejected without subsequently being charged.

According to the group's statement, officers later told those leadership members: 'We have nothing to legally charge you with, move on.'

The Cove alleged other supporters were also ejected without justification and accused police of antagonising fans rather than protecting them.

Daily Mail has contacted NSW Police for comment.

The Cove supporters' anger extended to Sydney FC, the APL and stadium officials, whom it challenged to intervene.

'Whilst you may stay silent and not fight for your fans, don't come crying if we don't show up,' the group said.

'Active support isn't a crime. Back your f*****g fans.'

At the centre of the dispute was The Cove's allegation that police ignored established arrangements for supporter marshals to help resolve issues in the stands.

The Cove accused police of bypassing supporter marshals during the October 16 clash with Western Sydney Wanderers

The group claimed marshalls and stadium security were overridden, with officers instead entering supporter bays and taking action without consultation.

'Nobody should be made to feel like a criminal for wanting to passionately support their club,' it said.

Sydney FC initially responded by saying it was investigating the allegations with Venues NSW, the APL and NSW Police.

A joint statement released by the club and The Cove on November 5 said subsequent discussions had produced a commitment to stronger communication, mutual respect and clearer matchday processes.

'All parties have agreed on the importance of active support to football in this country, and all believe passionate, active support and a safe matchday experience must go hand in hand,' it said.

The club thanked The Cove's leadership for its professional engagement, while the supporter group thanked Sydney FC for listening to members and standing alongside them.

The statement welcomed fans back but did not announce findings on the alleged derby incidents or specify changes to police operations.

In a subsequent Instagram post, The Cove said it wanted to ensure there was never a repeat of the round-one incidents.

The supporters will return for Sydney FC's clash with Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park

'We are hopeful that future policing at games will reflect the efforts made by the club, and Cove leadership,' it said.

'We will be monitoring the progress closely over the coming rounds.'

The dispute has also drawn intervention from the FSAA, which says supporters elsewhere in Australia and New Zealand share concerns about excessive police and security actions.

In an open letter published on November 5, the association welcomed Western Sydney Wanderers chairman Paul Lederer's criticism of police treatment of his club's fans.

It said APL leaders shared its frustration, but argued the response needed to go beyond discussions after each incident.

'We are now at the point where reactive reviews and weekly chats with police following regular operational failures on match day are simply insufficient,' the association wrote.

The FSAA said it had recommended structural changes in 2025, including rapid response protocols, measures to prevent supporters being demonised and better communication between authorities and fan groups.

It is now pushing for a framework involving senior league management, clubs, supporter leaders, stadium operators, private security and state police commands.
